check.question: Which mechanism mainly explains water rising in a tall tree on a hot day?
check.why: Rapid evaporation from the leaves creates the tension that pulls the water column upward.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Xylem is dead and carries water upward; phloem is living and carries food both ways. Transpiration pull is passive; active transport needs energy.

content.problem: A gardener removes a ring of bark from a young tree. Predict what happens above and below the ring.

steps.reason: The bark contains the phloem, which lies outside the xylem.
steps.result: Phloem transport is interrupted.
steps.predictPrompt: Which tissue remains able to carry water?

steps.reason: Sugars made in the leaves cannot pass down through the removed phloem.
steps.result: Sugars accumulate above the ring and the bark may swell.

steps.reason: The roots receive no sugars from the leaves.
steps.result: Root growth and respiration decline.

steps.reason: The root system starves while the shoot keeps photosynthesising.
steps.result: The tree may eventually die.

content.question: Why does a plant wilt on a hot, windy afternoon even when the soil is wet?
hints: Transpiration can remove water faster than roots absorb it.
Water loss lowers the turgor pressure that keeps leaves firm.
Wilting reduces water loss and can reverse when transpiration slows.

lessons.title: Diffusion, Osmosis and Water Relations
lessons.objective: Describe diffusion and osmosis, and explain plasmolysis and turgidity as the responses of plant cells to water movement.

content.heading: Diffusion, osmosis and water relations
paragraphs: A slice of fresh okra left in salt water goes limp within minutes. Water has crossed a membrane, and the direction of movement is the whole story.

content.heading: Diffusion: movement down a gradient
paragraphs: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. It is passive, so it uses the random motion of particles rather than energy from respiration.

Oxygen diffuses from the air in the lungs into blood, and from blood into respiring cells. Carbon (IV) oxide diffuses the other way. In a leaf, carbon (IV) oxide enters through stomata and oxygen leaves.

The rate depends on the concentration gradient, temperature, surface area and distance. Small, thin surfaces with a steep gradient speed diffusion up; that is why alveoli and root hairs are finely branched and thin.
bullets: Diffusion: particles move from high to low concentration.
It is passive and depends on random particle motion.
Steep gradients, large surfaces and short distances speed it up.
content.takeaway: Diffusion is passive movement from high to low concentration.

check.question: Diffusion is described as passive because it
options: Depends on the random movement of particles
check.why: Diffusion needs no metabolic energy; particles spread by their own random motion.

content.heading: Osmosis: water across a membrane
paragraphs: Osmosis is the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution. The dilute solution has more water molecules, so water moves toward the side with less water and more solute.
An animal cell placed in distilled water gains water and may burst; in strong salt solution it loses water and shrinks. A plant cell behaves differently because its cell wall resists expansion.
Root hairs use osmosis to absorb soil water, and water moves from cell to cell across the root. Osmosis is passive, but it depends on a water potential gradient and a membrane the water can cross.
bullets: Osmosis: water moves through a partially permeable membrane.
Water moves from dilute (high water) to concentrated (low water).
Animal cells may burst or shrink; plant cell walls resist expansion.
content.takeaway: Osmosis is water movement toward the more concentrated solution.

check.question: Water moves by osmosis from
options: A concentrated solution to a dilute solution
A dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
A region of low water potential to high water potential
Any cell to any other cell
check.why: Water moves down its own gradient, from the dilute side to the more concentrated side.

content.heading: Plasmolysis and turgidity
paragraphs: When a plant cell is in pure water, water enters its vacuole by osmosis. The vacuole swells, pushes the cytoplasm against the cell wall and the cell becomes turgid; turgor pressure keeps herbaceous plants upright.

In a concentrated salt or sugar solution, water leaves the vacuole. The protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall, and the cell is plasmolysed. The plant tissue becomes limp, which is why salted vegetables lose their crispness.

Plasmolysis is reversible if the cell is returned to water before the protoplast is badly damaged. Turgidity and plasmolysis explain wilting, food preservation with salt or sugar, and why fresh vegetables crisp up in cold water.
bullets: Turgid: water enters, vacuole swells, cell is firm.
Plasmolysed: water leaves, protoplast pulls away from the wall.
Turgidity supports plants; plasmolysis makes tissue limp.
content.takeaway: Turgid cells are firm; plasmolysed cells are limp.

check.question: A plant cell placed in concentrated salt solution will
options: Burst because it has no cell wall
Take in salt and become flaccid
check.why: The external solution is more concentrated, so water leaves the vacuole and the protoplast shrinks.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Diffusion moves any particles; osmosis moves only water through a membrane. Plasmolysis is the plant-cell result of water loss; turgidity is the result of water gain.

content.problem: Three potato strips are placed in distilled water, a dilute salt solution and a concentrated salt solution. Predict their firmness.

steps.reason: The cell sap is more concentrated than the surrounding water.
steps.result: Water enters by osmosis; the strip becomes turgid and firm.
steps.predictPrompt: What happens in the concentrated salt solution?

steps.reason: The gradient is small, so there is little net water movement.
steps.result: The strip stays firm, with little change in mass.

steps.reason: The external solution is more concentrated than the cell sap.
steps.result: Water leaves the cells; the strip becomes limp and plasmolysed.

content.question: Explain why a wilted lettuce leaf becomes crisp again when placed in cold water.
hints: The leaf cells have lost water and become flaccid.
The water outside is more dilute than the cell sap.
Water enters the vacuoles by osmosis and restores turgor pressure.

lessons.title: Respiration and Energy
lessons.objective: Explain the significance of respiration, describe ATP as the energy currency, and distinguish aerobic from anaerobic respiration.

content.heading: Respiration and energy
paragraphs: A sprinter leaves the blocks and is breathing hard ten seconds later. The muscles are spending energy that was stored in food and released inside cells.

content.heading: Respiration is not breathing
paragraphs: Respiration is the controlled release of energy from organic food inside cells. Breathing is only the movement of air that supplies oxygen and removes carbon (IV) oxide; respiration happens in every living cell, including cells with no lungs.

Glucose is broken down in a series of enzyme-controlled reactions. The energy released is used to make ATP, run active transport, build large molecules, contract muscles and keep the body warm. Some energy is always lost as heat.

Respiration is catabolic: it breaks larger molecules into simpler ones. Photosynthesis does the opposite, storing energy in glucose. The two processes are linked in a plant, and both depend on enzymes.
bullets: Respiration releases energy from food inside cells.
Breathing supplies oxygen and removes carbon (IV) oxide.
The released energy powers cell work, and some is lost as heat.
content.takeaway: Respiration is a chemical process in cells, not breathing.

check.question: Respiration is best described as the
options: Movement of air into the lungs
Controlled release of energy from food in cells
Loss of water vapour from leaves
Building of glucose from carbon (IV) oxide
check.why: Respiration is enzyme-controlled breakdown of food that releases energy for cell work.

content.heading: ATP: the energy currency
paragraphs: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is a small molecule that carries usable energy from respiration to the reactions that need it. When its terminal phosphate is removed, ATP becomes ADP and energy is released.
Cells can make ATP when needed and break it down at the same place, so energy is delivered in small packets rather than one large burst. This is why ATP is called the energy currency of the cell.

ATP powers muscle contraction, active transport, nerve impulses and the synthesis of proteins and other molecules. It is not a long-term store; the energy store is the food molecule, while ATP is the spendable form.
bullets: ATP carries energy from respiration to cell reactions.
Removing the terminal phosphate releases energy and leaves ADP.
ATP is spendable energy; food is the long-term store.
content.takeaway: Food stores energy; ATP spends it.

check.question: ATP releases useful energy when it is converted to
check.why: Breaking the terminal phosphate bond of ATP yields ADP, phosphate and usable energy.

content.heading: Aerobic and anaerobic at a glance
paragraphs: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and breaks glucose down completely to carbon (IV) oxide and water. It releases a large amount of ATP and happens mainly in the mitochondria.
Anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen. Glucose is only partly broken down, so less ATP is released; the products are lactic acid in muscles or ethanol and carbon (IV) oxide in yeast.
Both pathways begin with glycolysis in the cytoplasm. Oxygen decides which route follows, so the same glucose can yield very different amounts of energy depending on whether oxygen is present.
bullets: Aerobic: oxygen, complete breakdown, large ATP yield.
Anaerobic: no oxygen, partial breakdown, small ATP yield.
Products: lactic acid in muscles; ethanol and carbon (IV) oxide in yeast.
content.takeaway: Oxygen is the switch between high-yield aerobic and low-yield anaerobic respiration.

check.question: Which product is formed in anaerobic respiration in yeast but not in human muscle?
check.why: Yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol and carbon (IV) oxide, while human muscle forms lactic acid.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Respiration is a chemical process in cells, not breathing. Aerobic uses oxygen and makes much more ATP; anaerobic works without oxygen and makes much less.

content.problem: A student says a resting plant cannot respire because it is not breathing. Correct the statement and trace the energy.

steps.reason: Breathing is ventilation; respiration is a chemical reaction in cells.
steps.result: The plant respires even though it has no lungs.
steps.predictPrompt: How does a leaf exchange gases?

steps.reason: Leaves use stomata and woody stems use lenticels.
steps.result: Oxygen enters and carbon (IV) oxide leaves by diffusion.

steps.reason: Glucose is broken down and the energy is transferred to ATP.
steps.result: ATP powers the plant's active transport and growth.

steps.reason: Not all the energy is captured in ATP.
steps.result: Some is released as heat, even in a resting plant.

content.question: Why does a cell use ATP rather than spending glucose directly?
hints: Glucose is a stable storage molecule, not a ready payment.
ATP releases a small, controlled amount of energy.
Coupling ATP breakdown to cell reactions avoids a wasteful burst of heat.

lessons.title: Respiratory Organs and Surfaces
lessons.objective: Describe body surfaces, gills, tracheae, lungs, stomata and lenticels, and relate the features of a respiratory surface to efficient gas exchange.

content.heading: Respiratory organs and surfaces
paragraphs: A fish in a Lagos lagoon and a grasshopper on the bank both need oxygen, but neither has a lung. Their surfaces show how anatomy follows habitat.

content.heading: What makes a good respiratory surface
paragraphs: Gas exchange happens by diffusion, so a respiratory surface must be thin, moist and permeable. It also needs a large surface area and a steep concentration gradient, usually maintained by ventilation or blood flow.

These features are summarized in Fick's law: the rate of diffusion is proportional to surface area and concentration difference, and inversely proportional to thickness. A thick, dry surface slows exchange.
Terrestrial surfaces lose water easily, so land animals keep their exchange surfaces inside the body. Aquatic animals can use exposed gills because water supports them and prevents drying.
bullets: Thin, moist and permeable for fast diffusion.
Large area and a steep concentration gradient for more exchange.
Ventilation and blood flow maintain the gradient.
content.takeaway: Thin, moist, large and well supplied: the four tests of a respiratory surface.

check.question: Which feature would decrease the rate of gas exchange across a surface?
check.why: Thickness and dryness increase diffusion distance and slow gas exchange.

content.heading: Body surface, gills and tracheae
paragraphs: An Amoeba exchanges gases over its whole body surface. An earthworm uses moist skin, kept thin and vascular by mucus and a good blood supply. These surfaces work only where the distance is short and the body is not too thick.

Fish use gills with many thin lamellae. Water flows over the gills in the opposite direction to blood, a countercurrent arrangement that keeps a concentration gradient along the whole gill and extracts more oxygen.

Insects use tracheae: air enters through spiracles, travels along tubes and reaches cells through fine tracheoles. This system delivers oxygen directly, so insect blood does not need haemoglobin for most gas transport.
bullets: Body surface: Amoeba and earthworm, thin and moist.
Gills: fish, many lamellae with countercurrent water and blood flow.
Tracheae: insects, air delivered directly to cells through tracheoles.
content.takeaway: Body surface suits small animals; gills suit water; tracheae pipe air directly.

check.question: The countercurrent flow in fish gills
options: Makes water and blood flow in the same direction
Maintains a concentration gradient along the gill
Cools the fish in warm water
check.why: Opposite flows keep oxygen diffusing into the blood along the whole length of the gill.

content.heading: Lungs, stomata and lenticels
paragraphs: Mammals use lungs, where millions of alveoli give a huge, thin, moist surface. Each alveolus is surrounded by capillaries, and ventilation plus blood flow keeps oxygen coming in and carbon (IV) oxide leaving.
Plants have no lungs. Leaves exchange gases through stomata, each guarded by two guard cells; woody stems use lenticels, and roots absorb oxygen through root hairs and air spaces in the soil.
The exchange surface matches the habitat: moist skin in damp soil, gills in water, tracheae in air, alveoli in a sealed lung. The same diffusion rules apply to all of them.
bullets: Lungs: alveoli give a large, thin, moist surface with capillaries.
Leaves use stomata; woody stems use lenticels; roots use air spaces.
Every surface follows the same diffusion rules.
content.takeaway: The surface follows the habitat, but diffusion follows the same rules.

check.question: Which structure is the respiratory surface of a woody stem?
check.why: Lenticels are loose patches of cells in the bark that allow gas exchange.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Match the surface to the organism: moist skin for earthworm, gills for fish, tracheae for insects, alveoli for mammals, stomata and lenticels for plants.

content.problem: An unknown animal has moist skin, no lungs and lives in damp soil. Identify its respiratory surface and explain why it cannot live in dry sand.

steps.reason: The whole body surface is thin, moist and supplied with blood.
steps.result: Body surface, as in an earthworm.
steps.predictPrompt: What happens to that surface in dry air?

steps.reason: The surface must stay moist for oxygen to dissolve and diffuse.
steps.result: Dry sand would dry the skin and stop gas exchange.

steps.reason: The animal has no internal lung to protect its surface from drying.
steps.result: It is restricted to damp soil or water.

content.question: Why does a fish die when it is taken out of water, even though air contains more oxygen than water?
hints: Gill lamellae are supported by water and collapse in air.
Collapsed lamellae greatly reduce the exposed surface area.
The gill surface also dries, so oxygen cannot dissolve.

lessons.title: Gas Exchange in Plants
lessons.objective: Describe the opening and closing of stomata, identify lenticels and root surfaces as gas-exchange routes, and compare leaf gas exchange in light and darkness.

content.heading: Gas exchange in plants
paragraphs: A maize leaf at noon is losing water through thousands of tiny pores while it takes in carbon (IV) oxide. The same pores must balance food-making against water loss.

content.heading: Stomata and the guard cells
paragraphs: Each stoma is a pore between two guard cells. Guard cells are kidney-shaped, have thicker inner walls and contain chloroplasts. When they take up water and become turgid, they bow outward and the pore opens; when they lose water, they become flaccid and the pore closes.
The movement is driven by osmosis. Potassium ions enter the guard cells, lowering their water potential so water follows; when potassium leaves, water leaves and the pore shuts.

Stomata usually open in light and close in darkness or drought. This lets carbon (IV) oxide enter for photosynthesis while limiting water loss, but the balance changes with humidity, temperature and wind.
bullets: Stoma: a pore between two guard cells.
Turgid guard cells open the pore; flaccid guard cells close it.
Potassium ions and osmosis drive the opening and closing.
content.takeaway: Guard cells open the pore when turgid and close it when flaccid.

check.question: A stoma opens when its guard cells
options: Take in water and become turgid
Are covered by a waxy cuticle
check.why: Water uptake makes the guard cells turgid and their curved walls pull the pore open.

content.heading: Lenticels, roots and other surfaces
paragraphs: Most gas exchange in a leaf happens through stomata, but the leaf surface is covered by a waxy cuticle that limits diffusion. The stomata are therefore the main controllable gates.

Woody stems have lenticels, loose patches of cells in the bark that let oxygen in and carbon (IV) oxide out. Roots take up oxygen from air spaces in the soil, and root hairs increase the surface for this exchange.
Submerged plants may have no stomata and exchange gases over thin leaves, while floating leaves keep stomata on the upper surface. The surface is positioned where the gas supply is.
bullets: Leaves: stomata through the cuticle.
Woody stems: lenticels in the bark.
Roots: root hairs and air spaces in the soil.
content.takeaway: Stomata serve leaves, lenticels serve stems, and root surfaces serve roots.

check.question: Which surface allows gas exchange in a woody stem?
check.why: Lenticels are loose patches in the bark that connect the stem's air spaces to the atmosphere.

content.heading: Day and night in the leaf
paragraphs: In daylight, photosynthesis is usually faster than respiration. The leaf takes in carbon (IV) oxide and releases oxygen, so the net exchange hides the respiration that is still going on.
At night, photosynthesis stops but respiration continues. The leaf takes in oxygen and releases carbon (IV) oxide, which is why a respiring plant can be shown with limewater in the dark.
Respiration in plants also produces heat and uses stored food. The gas exchange of the whole plant depends on stomata, lenticels and root surfaces working together, not on one organ.
bullets: Day: photosynthesis dominates; carbon (IV) oxide enters and oxygen leaves.
Night: respiration dominates; oxygen enters and carbon (IV) oxide leaves.
Limewater turns milky when carbon (IV) oxide is bubbled through it.
content.takeaway: In light the leaf gains carbon and loses oxygen; at night the direction reverses.

check.question: At night, a leaf releases more
check.why: Photosynthesis stops at night, so respiration releases carbon (IV) oxide and uses oxygen.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Stomata open when turgid and close when flaccid. In light, net gas exchange follows photosynthesis; at night, respiration dominates.

content.problem: A potted plant is sealed in a clear container with limewater and kept in the dark. Predict what happens to the limewater and why.

steps.reason: Photosynthesis cannot run without light.
steps.result: The plant stops taking in carbon (IV) oxide.
steps.predictPrompt: Does respiration stop too?

steps.reason: Respiration continues day and night in living cells.
steps.result: The plant releases carbon (IV) oxide into the container.

steps.reason: Carbon (IV) oxide reacts with limewater.
steps.result: The limewater turns milky.

content.question: Why do stomata close on a hot, dry afternoon even though photosynthesis needs carbon (IV) oxide?
hints: Open stomata lose water vapour as well as exchange gases.
Water loss lowers guard-cell turgor and can wilt the leaf.
Closing the stomata protects the plant from drying out.

lessons.title: Aerobic Respiration
lessons.objective: Outline glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain, and explain how oxygen allows a large ATP yield.

content.heading: Aerobic respiration
paragraphs: A runner's muscles keep working long after the first few seconds because oxygen is available. Aerobic respiration unlocks most of the energy in glucose in three linked stages.

content.heading: Glycolysis in the cytoplasm
paragraphs: Glycolysis is the first stage of both aerobic and anaerobic respiration. It happens in the cytoplasm and does not need oxygen. One glucose molecule (6 carbons) is split into two pyruvate molecules (3 carbons each).
The process uses two ATP to start and produces four ATP, so the net gain is two ATP. It also transfers energy to NADH, which will carry electrons to later stages.
Glycolysis is a chain of enzyme-controlled steps, not a single explosion. Because it can run without oxygen, it gives a cell a quick supply of ATP when oxygen is short.
bullets: Location: cytoplasm; oxygen not required.
Glucose (6C) splits into two pyruvate (3C) molecules.
Net gain: 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.
content.takeaway: Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate and gives a small net ATP gain.

check.question: The net ATP yield of glycolysis per glucose molecule is
check.why: Four ATP are made but two are used to start glycolysis, leaving a net gain of two.

content.heading: The Krebs cycle in the mitochondrion
paragraphs: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is converted to acetyl CoA, releasing carbon (IV) oxide and forming NADH. Acetyl CoA then enters the Krebs cycle in the matrix.
In the Krebs cycle, acetyl CoA joins a four-carbon acceptor to make a six-carbon acid. The acid is broken down in steps, releasing carbon (IV) oxide and transferring energy to ATP, NADH and FADH2.
Each glucose produces two turns of the cycle. The cycle itself makes only a small amount of ATP directly; most of the energy is now carried by NADH and FADH2 to the inner membrane.
bullets: Pyruvate is converted to acetyl CoA, releasing carbon (IV) oxide.
The Krebs cycle turns twice per glucose and releases more carbon (IV) oxide.
It makes a little ATP and loads NADH and FADH2 with energy.
content.takeaway: Krebs strips carbon and loads electron carriers.

check.question: Where does the Krebs cycle take place?
check.why: The enzymes of the Krebs cycle are in the mitochondrial matrix.

content.heading: Oxygen and the electron transport chain
paragraphs: NADH and FADH2 deliver electrons to the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane. As electrons pass along the chain, energy pumps protons and the return flow drives ATP synthesis.

Oxygen is the final electron acceptor. It combines with electrons and protons to form water, and this step keeps the chain running; without oxygen, the carriers stay reduced and the whole aerobic pathway stalls.

The complete breakdown of one glucose yields carbon (IV) oxide, water and a large amount of ATP, often quoted as 36-38 ATP in textbooks. Some energy is released as heat, which helps maintain body temperature.
bullets: Electron transport chain: inner mitochondrial membrane.
Oxygen accepts the final electrons and forms water.
Most ATP is made here; some energy is lost as heat.
content.takeaway: Oxygen accepts the last electrons and lets the ATP pipeline run.

check.question: The role of oxygen in aerobic respiration is to
options: Accept the final electrons and form water
Make carbon (IV) oxide in the Krebs cycle
Carry electrons to the Krebs cycle
check.why: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Glycolysis gives 2 ATP; Krebs gives a little more; the electron transport chain gives most. Oxygen is needed only at the last stage.

content.problem: One glucose molecule yields 2 ATP in glycolysis and 2 ATP in the Krebs cycle. The electron transport chain brings the textbook total to 38 ATP. How many ATP come from the chain, and why does oxygen matter?

steps.reason: Glycolysis and Krebs make ATP directly.
steps.predictPrompt: Where is the rest of the energy released?

steps.reason: The total is 38 ATP, so subtract the direct yield.
steps.result: 38 - 4 = 34 ATP from the electron transport chain.

steps.reason: Oxygen accepts the final electrons and keeps the chain running.
steps.result: Without oxygen the chain stops and the large ATP yield is lost.

content.question: Why does a muscle cell switch to anaerobic respiration when oxygen runs out?
hints: The electron transport chain needs oxygen as the final electron acceptor.
Without oxygen, NADH cannot be reoxidised to NAD+.
Glycolysis can continue only if NAD+ is regenerated, so pyruvate is converted to lactic acid.

lessons.title: Anaerobic Respiration and Fermentation
lessons.objective: Explain lactic acid formation and oxygen debt in muscles, describe fermentation in yeast, and compare aerobic with anaerobic respiration.

content.heading: Anaerobic respiration and fermentation
paragraphs: A sprinter finishes a race gasping for air, while a bowl of dough rises quietly on a kitchen table. Both are using anaerobic respiration, but their products are different.

content.heading: Lactic acid in muscles
paragraphs: During hard exercise, muscles may use oxygen faster than blood can deliver it. Glycolysis continues, but pyruvate is converted to lactic acid instead of entering the Krebs cycle, so only two ATP are gained per glucose.

Lactic acid lowers the pH of muscle tissue and contributes to fatigue and cramp. The muscle is not poisoned permanently; when oxygen returns, some lactic acid is oxidised to carbon (IV) oxide and water, and some is converted back to glucose in the liver.
The extra oxygen needed after exercise to remove lactic acid is called the oxygen debt. Breathing stays fast because the body is repaying that debt, not because the muscles are still working hard.
bullets: Muscle anaerobic respiration: glucose to lactic acid, net 2 ATP.
Lactic acid contributes to fatigue and cramp.
Oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed to remove lactic acid.
content.takeaway: No oxygen means lactate, two ATP and an oxygen debt.

check.question: The product of anaerobic respiration in human muscle is
check.why: Human muscle converts pyruvate to lactic acid when oxygen is insufficient.

content.heading: Ethanol and carbon (IV) oxide in yeast
paragraphs: Yeast is a single-celled fungus that respires aerobically when oxygen is present but ferments sugar when oxygen is low. Glycolysis yields two ATP, and the pyruvate is then converted to ethanol and carbon (IV) oxide.

Fermentation is anaerobic respiration in yeast and some other microbes. The carbon (IV) oxide makes bread dough rise, while the ethanol evaporates during baking; in palm wine, beer and wine, ethanol is the product people want.
Yeast is also used to make bioethanol, yeast extract, vitamins and animal feed. Its ability to ferment sugar is therefore economically important in food, drink and fuel production.
bullets: Yeast fermentation: glucose to ethanol + carbon (IV) oxide, net 2 ATP.
Carbon (IV) oxide raises bread dough; ethanol is the aim in drinks and fuel.
Yeast is economically important in food, drink and bioethanol production.
content.takeaway: Yeast turns sugar into ethanol, carbon (IV) oxide and a little ATP.

check.question: Which gas makes bread dough rise during yeast fermentation?
check.why: Carbon (IV) oxide released by yeast forms bubbles that expand the dough.

content.heading: Aerobic versus anaerobic
paragraphs: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen, breaks glucose completely and yields about 36-38 ATP. Anaerobic respiration needs no oxygen, breaks glucose only partly and yields two ATP, so it is much less efficient per glucose molecule.

Aerobic respiration happens mainly in mitochondria and releases carbon (IV) oxide and water. Anaerobic respiration happens in the cytoplasm and releases lactic acid in muscle, or ethanol and carbon (IV) oxide in yeast and waterlogged roots.
Anaerobic respiration is fast and useful in short bursts, but the waste products limit it. Aerobic respiration is slower to start but sustains long activity because it releases far more energy.
bullets: Aerobic: oxygen, mitochondria, complete breakdown, about 36-38 ATP.
Anaerobic: no oxygen, cytoplasm, partial breakdown, 2 ATP.
Anaerobic is fast but wasteful; aerobic sustains long activity.
content.takeaway: Aerobic is efficient but oxygen-dependent; anaerobic is fast but wasteful.

check.question: Which statement correctly compares aerobic and anaerobic respiration?
options: Aerobic releases more ATP per glucose than anaerobic
Anaerobic releases more ATP per glucose than aerobic
Both release the same amount of ATP per glucose
Anaerobic requires oxygen but aerobic does not
check.why: Complete aerobic breakdown releases far more ATP than partial anaerobic breakdown.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Muscle anaerobic gives lactic acid with no carbon (IV) oxide. Yeast anaerobic gives ethanol plus carbon (IV) oxide. Both yield 2 ATP per glucose.

content.problem: A sealed flask of yeast and glucose solution is connected to limewater. Predict two observations and explain them.

steps.reason: Yeast ferments glucose and releases carbon (IV) oxide.
steps.result: Bubbles appear in the flask and gas travels to the limewater.
steps.predictPrompt: What will the limewater do?

steps.reason: Carbon (IV) oxide turns limewater milky.
steps.result: The limewater becomes milky.

steps.reason: The flask is sealed, so oxygen is soon used up and fermentation takes over.
steps.result: Ethanol is formed, giving a characteristic smell.

content.question: Why does a sprinter breathe heavily after a race rather than only during the first few seconds?
hints: The muscles built up lactic acid while oxygen was short.
Extra oxygen is needed to oxidise the lactic acid.
The fast breathing after exercise is repaying the oxygen debt.

lessons.title: Excretion and Excretory Products
lessons.objective: Define excretion, distinguish it from egestion and secretion, explain its significance, and compare ammonia, urea and uric acid as nitrogenous wastes.

content.heading: Excretion and excretory products
paragraphs: A patient with kidney failure becomes drowsy when wastes build up in the blood. The body's cleaning system has stopped working.

content.heading: Excretion is not egestion
paragraphs: Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste products from the body. These wastes are made inside cells, such as carbon (IV) oxide from respiration and urea from the breakdown of excess amino acids.

Egestion is different: it is the removal of undigested food from the alimentary canal, and the material was never part of the body's metabolism. Secretion is also different, because it releases useful substances such as enzymes and hormones.
Excretion therefore includes lungs, kidneys, skin and plant stomata, but not the rectum. A useful substance released by a gland is a secretion, even though it leaves the cell.
bullets: Excretion: metabolic wastes such as carbon (IV) oxide and urea.
Egestion: undigested food removed as faeces.
Secretion: useful substances such as enzymes and hormones.
content.takeaway: Excretion removes metabolic waste; egestion removes unabsorbed food.

check.question: Which process removes undigested food from the body?
check.why: Egestion removes unabsorbed food from the alimentary canal; it was never part of metabolism.

content.heading: Why excretion matters
paragraphs: Metabolic wastes can be toxic. Carbon (IV) oxide lowers blood pH, urea raises the concentration of nitrogenous waste, and excess salts disturb the balance of water between cells and blood.
Excretion keeps the internal environment steady: water balance, salt balance, pH and temperature. This steady state is called homeostasis, and the kidneys are its main control organs in mammals.

If excretion fails, wastes accumulate and cells cannot work properly. Dialysis can temporarily remove urea and excess salts from the blood when the kidneys fail, but it does not replace every kidney function.
bullets: Wastes can be toxic and disturb pH and water balance.
Excretion helps maintain homeostasis.
Dialysis removes some wastes but is not a full substitute for kidneys.
content.takeaway: Excretion protects cells by keeping the internal environment steady.

check.question: The main control organs of water and salt balance in mammals are the
check.why: The kidneys filter blood and adjust water and salt reabsorption to control urine concentration.

content.heading: Nitrogenous wastes: ammonia, urea and uric acid
paragraphs: Ammonia is formed when amino acids are broken down. It is very soluble and highly toxic, so aquatic animals such as fish can release it directly into water, where it is quickly diluted.

Land animals convert ammonia to urea in the liver. Urea is less toxic and needs less water to excrete, which suits mammals; birds, reptiles and insects convert it to uric acid, a semi-solid paste that conserves even more water.
The choice reflects habitat: ammonia needs plenty of water, urea needs moderate water, and uric acid needs little. The trade-off is that making urea and uric acid costs energy.
bullets: Ammonia: very soluble, toxic, released by fish into water.
Urea: less toxic, made in the liver, excreted by mammals.
Uric acid: semi-solid, conserves water, used by birds, reptiles and insects.
content.takeaway: Ammonia is fast and watery; urea is balanced; uric acid saves water.

check.question: Which nitrogenous waste is least soluble and conserves the most water?
check.why: Uric acid is excreted as a semi-solid paste, which limits water loss.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Excretion is metabolic waste; egestion is undigested food. Ammonia suits fish, urea suits mammals, and uric acid suits birds, reptiles and insects.

content.problem: A student says faeces are an excretory product. Correct the statement and classify three wastes.

steps.reason: Faeces contain unabsorbed food that never entered cell metabolism.
steps.result: Faeces are removed by egestion, not excretion.
steps.predictPrompt: How should carbon (IV) oxide be classified?

steps.reason: It is made during respiration inside cells.
steps.result: An excretory product removed by the lungs.

steps.reason: It is made in the liver from excess amino acids.
steps.result: An excretory product removed by the kidneys.

content.question: Why do desert reptiles excrete uric acid rather than ammonia?
hints: Ammonia is highly toxic and very soluble.
Excreting ammonia would require a lot of water.
Uric acid is semi-solid and conserves water, though making it costs energy.

lessons.title: Excretory Structures
lessons.objective: Relate the structure of contractile vacuoles, flame cells, nephridia, Malpighian tubules, kidneys, stomata and lenticels to their excretory functions.

content.heading: Excretory structures
paragraphs: A pond Amoeba, a tapeworm, an earthworm and a grasshopper all get rid of wastes without owning a kidney. Each has a different solution.

content.heading: Contractile vacuole, flame cell and nephridium
paragraphs: An Amoeba lives in fresh water, where water constantly enters by osmosis. Its contractile vacuole collects the excess water and expels it, preventing the cell from bursting; the same organelle removes some dissolved wastes.

A flame cell is a hollow cell with a tuft of cilia that beats like a flame. It drives fluid through a network of tubules in flatworms such as Taenia, filtering wastes while useful materials are reabsorbed.
A nephridium is a coiled tubule in an earthworm. It opens into the body cavity, takes up coelomic fluid, reabsorbs useful salts and water, and releases urine through a pore in the body wall.
bullets: Contractile vacuole: collects and expels excess water.
Flame cell: ciliated cell that drives fluid through tubules in flatworms.
Nephridium: coiled tubule that filters coelomic fluid in earthworms.
content.takeaway: Contractile vacuole pumps water; flame cells and nephridia filter body fluid.

check.question: Which structure prevents a freshwater Amoeba from bursting?
check.why: The contractile vacuole expels excess water that enters the cell by osmosis.

content.heading: Malpighian tubules and kidneys
paragraphs: Insects use Malpighian tubules, fine tubes that open into the gut. They take up uric acid and salts from the body fluid and empty them into the hindgut, where water is reabsorbed and the waste leaves with faeces.
The vertebrate kidney is a compact organ packed with nephrons. Each nephron filters blood under pressure, reabsorbs useful glucose, salts and water, and leaves urea and excess ions in the urine.

The structures get more complex with body size: a contractile vacuole in a single cell, flame cells and nephridia in worms, Malpighian tubules in insects, and paired kidneys in vertebrates. The principle is the same: remove waste and reclaim what is useful.
bullets: Malpighian tubules: take up uric acid and empty it into the hindgut.
Kidney nephrons: filter blood, reabsorb useful materials, leave urine.
The structures become more complex as body size increases.
content.takeaway: Filter, reabsorb, then excrete: the same logic at every level.

check.question: Malpighian tubules empty waste into the
check.why: Malpighian tubules connect to the hindgut, where water is reabsorbed before waste is passed out.

content.heading: Stomata and lenticels
paragraphs: Plants do not have kidneys. Their main excretory surfaces are stomata in leaves and lenticels in woody stems, which release carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour and allow oxygen to leave.
Some plant wastes are stored rather than expelled. Tannins, resins, gums, mucilage and alkaloids are kept in vacuoles, ducts or specialized cells, and may be released when the plant is damaged.

Storage protects the plant from its own toxic products and can also deter herbivores. The excretory structure therefore matches the organism: a pump in a protist, a tubule in a worm, a kidney in a mammal, and a pore in a leaf.
bullets: Stomata and lenticels release gases and water vapour.
Tannins, resins, gums, mucilage and alkaloids may be stored.
Storage protects the plant and can deter herbivores.
content.takeaway: Animal excretory organs filter; plant surfaces release or store wastes.

check.question: Which pair are plant excretory surfaces?
check.why: Leaves use stomata and woody stems use lenticels for gas and water-vapour exchange.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Contractile vacuole = water; flame cell or nephridium = filtered body fluid; Malpighian tubule = uric acid; kidney = urea; stoma or lenticel = gases and water vapour.

content.problem: Match each organism to its excretory structure: Amoeba, earthworm, grasshopper and mammal.

steps.reason: A single freshwater cell must expel water that enters by osmosis.
steps.result: Contractile vacuole.
steps.predictPrompt: Which structure serves the earthworm?

steps.reason: Coelomic fluid is filtered by coiled tubules that open to the outside.
steps.result: Nephridia.

steps.reason: Fine tubules take up uric acid and empty it into the hindgut.
steps.result: Malpighian tubules.

steps.reason: Blood is filtered under pressure and useful materials are reabsorbed.
steps.result: Kidneys with nephrons.

content.question: Why are Malpighian tubules well suited to insects living on land?
hints: Insects must conserve water.
The tubules excrete uric acid rather than ammonia.
Water is reabsorbed from the hindgut before the waste is passed out.

lessons.title: The Mammalian Kidney
lessons.objective: Relate the structure of the kidney and nephron to ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption and osmoregulation.

content.heading: The mammalian kidney
paragraphs: A football match in Kano leaves a player thirsty and passing concentrated urine. The kidneys are adjusting water loss to keep the blood steady.

content.heading: Kidney structure
paragraphs: The kidneys are a pair of bean-shaped organs behind the abdominal cavity, supplied by the renal artery and drained by the renal vein. Each kidney has an outer cortex, an inner medulla and a central pelvis that leads to the ureter.

The functional unit is the nephron; a kidney contains about a million of them. The nephron begins with a glomerulus inside a Bowman's capsule and continues through the proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule and collecting duct.

Blood enters the glomerulus at high pressure and leaves through the efferent arteriole, while the filtrate passes along the tubule. The arrangement of cortex, medulla and pelvis is what lets the kidney filter, reabsorb and then drain urine.
bullets: Cortex outside, medulla inside, renal pelvis draining to the ureter.
The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.
Glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, tubules and collecting duct form the nephron.
content.takeaway: Cortex filters, medulla concentrates, pelvis drains.

check.question: The functional unit of the kidney is the
check.why: Each nephron filters blood and modifies the filtrate to form urine.

content.heading: Ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption
paragraphs: In ultrafiltration, blood pressure in the glomerulus forces water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea through the capillary wall and capsule into the nephron. Blood cells and large proteins remain in the blood because they are too large.

Selective reabsorption follows. The proximal tubule uses active transport and osmosis to reclaim glucose, amino acids, most salts and much of the water; its cells have microvilli and many mitochondria for this work.

The loop of Henle creates a salt gradient in the medulla, and the collecting duct uses that gradient to reabsorb more water. Anything not reabsorbed, mainly urea, excess salts and water, leaves as urine through the ureter, bladder and urethra.
bullets: Ultrafiltration: pressure forces small molecules into Bowman's capsule.
Selective reabsorption: glucose, amino acids, salts and water are reclaimed.
Urine contains urea, excess salts and water, not glucose or protein.
content.takeaway: Filter under pressure, then take back what the body still needs.

check.question: Which substance is normally absent from urine?
check.why: Glucose is normally reabsorbed completely in the proximal tubule.

content.heading: Osmoregulation
paragraphs: Osmoregulation is the control of water and salt balance. When a person is dehydrated, the hypothalamus detects rising blood solute concentration and the posterior pituitary releases more ADH.

ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed and a small amount of concentrated urine is produced. When a person drinks plenty of water, ADH falls and dilute urine is produced.

The kidney therefore controls both excretion and water balance. Alcohol and some drugs increase urine output by reducing ADH, while kidney failure reduces filtration and allows urea to accumulate in blood.
bullets: Dehydration raises ADH; ADH increases water reabsorption.
Hydration lowers ADH; more dilute urine is produced.
Kidney failure reduces filtration and causes waste accumulation.
content.takeaway: ADH tells the collecting duct to save water.

check.question: ADH increases water reabsorption by acting on the
check.why: ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable, so more water returns to the blood.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Ultrafiltration keeps cells and proteins; reabsorption keeps glucose and useful salts; ADH keeps water. Urine normally contains urea, salts and water, not glucose.

content.problem: A patient's urine contains glucose and protein. Explain what each result suggests about the nephron.

steps.reason: Glucose should be reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, or filtered only when blood glucose is very high.
steps.result: The tubule may be damaged, or the blood glucose may exceed the reabsorption limit.
steps.predictPrompt: Where should protein be stopped?

steps.reason: Large proteins should not pass through the glomerular filter.
steps.result: Protein in urine suggests damage to the filtration barrier.

steps.reason: Two abnormal findings point to a kidney problem rather than a normal variation.
steps.result: The patient needs medical tests to locate the damage.

content.question: Why does a dehydrated person produce less urine?
hints: Blood solute concentration rises when water is lost.
The posterior pituitary releases more ADH.
The collecting ducts reabsorb more water, leaving concentrated urine.

lessons.title: Lungs and Skin as Excretory Organs
lessons.objective: Identify the excretory products and functions of the lungs and skin, and explain how sweating and skin blood flow control body temperature.

content.heading: Lungs and skin as excretory organs
paragraphs: After a long run in Lagos, a runner's breath is moist and his shirt is wet with sweat. The lungs and skin are both disposing of waste.

content.heading: Lungs: carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour
paragraphs: The lungs are the excretory route for carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour. Carbon (IV) oxide is made in every respiring cell, carried in blood to the lungs and diffused into the alveoli to be breathed out.
Water vapour is lost with every exhale because the alveolar surface is moist. The lungs also lose heat, which is why breathing hard in a cold room produces visible vapour.
Lungs are not a route for urea. Their excretory role is tied to respiration and the need to keep blood pH stable; too much carbon (IV) oxide lowers pH and triggers faster breathing.
bullets: Lungs excrete carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour.
They also lose heat with each breath.
Lungs do not excrete urea; they help control blood pH.
content.takeaway: Lungs excrete carbon (IV) oxide, water vapour and heat.

check.question: The main excretory product removed by the lungs is
check.why: Carbon (IV) oxide produced by respiration is carried to the lungs and breathed out.

content.heading: Skin: sweat and temperature control
paragraphs: The skin has sweat glands in the dermis. Each gland coils below the surface and opens at a pore; its secretion, sweat, contains water, salts, urea and lactic acid.
Sweating removes small amounts of nitrogenous waste, but its main job is cooling. As sweat evaporates it takes latent heat from the skin, helping to keep body temperature near 37°C.
Blood vessels in the skin widen in heat and narrow in cold. Wider vessels bring more blood to the surface for heat loss, while narrower vessels keep heat in the core; shivering generates extra heat.
bullets: Sweat contains water, salts, urea and lactic acid.
Evaporation of sweat removes latent heat and cools the body.
Vasodilation loses heat; vasoconstriction and shivering conserve or make heat.
content.takeaway: Sweat cools the body and carries a little urea and salt.

check.question: The main function of sweating is to
options: Remove all urea from the blood
check.why: Evaporating sweat takes latent heat from the skin and lowers body temperature.

content.heading: Working with the kidneys
paragraphs: The kidneys are the main excretory organs for urea and salts, but the lungs, skin and gut also remove wastes. Lungs remove carbon (IV) oxide, skin removes some urea and salts, and the gut removes bile pigments in faeces.

When kidneys fail, urea accumulates and the skin may carry more urea in sweat, but sweating cannot replace filtration. Dialysis takes over part of the kidney's work by cleaning blood outside the body.
Excretion is therefore a team effort: each organ removes the waste it is suited to handle, and together they keep the internal environment stable.
bullets: Kidneys: main route for urea and excess salts.
Lungs: carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour.
Skin and gut: small contributions; dialysis supports failing kidneys.
content.takeaway: Lungs handle volatile waste, skin handles water and some urea, kidneys do the main filtration.

check.question: Which organ is the main route for urea excretion?
check.why: The kidneys filter urea from blood and excrete it in urine.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Lungs = carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour; skin = water, salts, urea and heat; kidneys = urea and excess salts. Do not credit the lungs with urea.

content.problem: A patient with kidney failure sweats heavily and has urea on the skin. Explain why this does not solve the problem.

steps.reason: Sweat carries water, salts and a small amount of urea.
steps.result: Only a tiny fraction of the waste is removed.
steps.predictPrompt: Can the skin filter blood?

steps.reason: The kidney filters the whole blood volume and adjusts reabsorption.
steps.result: Sweating cannot control urea concentration or water balance.

steps.reason: The failing kidney needs filtration to be replaced.
steps.result: Dialysis or a kidney transplant is required.

content.question: Why does the skin become red and sweaty during heavy exercise?
hints: Muscles produce extra heat during exercise.
Vasodilation brings more blood to the skin surface.
Sweat evaporation removes latent heat and cools the body.

lessons.title: Plant Excretion and Its Products
lessons.objective: Identify the excretory products of plants, including gases and stored chemicals, and explain their economic importance.

content.heading: Plant excretion and its products
paragraphs: A rubber tapper cuts a tree and collects a milky sap; a carpenter smells resin in pine wood. Plants make and store many chemicals that people use.

content.heading: Gases and water vapour
paragraphs: Plants excrete carbon (IV) oxide, oxygen and water vapour through stomata and lenticels. Carbon (IV) oxide is a product of respiration, while oxygen is a by-product of photosynthesis and leaves during the day.

These gases are not waste to every organism. Oxygen supports respiration in animals and is used in hospitals, while carbon (IV) oxide is used by plants for photosynthesis and in soft drinks and fire extinguishers.

Water vapour is also lost through transpiration, though the main stored excretory products discussed here are the organic chemicals. The plant cannot store these gases, so they diffuse out as soon as they are made.
bullets: Carbon (IV) oxide is released by respiration.
Oxygen is released by photosynthesis during the day.
Water vapour leaves through stomata and lenticels.
content.takeaway: Plants release gases and water vapour through stomata and lenticels.

check.question: Which gas is released by photosynthesis and excreted through stomata?
check.why: Oxygen is a by-product of photosynthesis and diffuses out through the stomata.

content.heading: Tannins, resins, gums and mucilage
paragraphs: Tannins are bitter phenolic compounds stored in vacuoles and bark. They deter herbivores and microbes, and people use them to tan leather, make dyes and produce astringent medicines.
Resins are sticky mixtures secreted into ducts, especially in conifers. They seal wounds and repel insects, and are used in varnishes, adhesives, incense and some medicines.

Gums and mucilage are polysaccharides that swell in water. Gums exuded from acacia and other trees are used as adhesives, thickeners and emulsifiers; mucilage from okra and cactus holds water and soothes irritated tissue.
bullets: Tannins: tan leather, make dyes and astringent medicines.
Resins: seal wounds; used in varnish, adhesives and incense.
Gums and mucilage: thicken, emulsify and hold water.
content.takeaway: Tannins tan, resins seal, gums glue and mucilage thickens.

check.question: Which plant product is used to tan leather?
check.why: Tannins bind to proteins in animal hides and preserve them as leather.

content.heading: Alkaloids and the economic ledger
paragraphs: Alkaloids are nitrogen-containing compounds that taste bitter and often affect the nervous system. Plants store them in leaves, bark, roots or seeds, where they deter herbivores and kill microbes.

Many alkaloids are medicines in the right dose: quinine from cinchona treats malaria, morphine from opium poppy relieves pain, and caffeine from coffee is a stimulant. Nicotine from tobacco is an insecticide but is harmful to people.
The economic importance of plant excretions is therefore double-edged. They provide medicines, tannins, resins, gums, dyes and food additives, but some are toxic and must be used carefully.
bullets: Alkaloids are bitter, nitrogen-containing defensive compounds.
Quinine, morphine and caffeine are useful alkaloids.
Some alkaloids are toxic, so dose and preparation matter.
content.takeaway: Plant wastes become medicines, materials and poisons depending on dose.

check.question: Quinine, used to treat malaria, is obtained from
check.why: Quinine is an alkaloid extracted from the bark of the cinchona tree.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Tannins tan leather, resins make varnish and incense, gums and mucilage thicken, and alkaloids include quinine and morphine. Plants also excrete oxygen, carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour.

content.problem: A factory wants to use local plant waste. Evaluate three options: tannin-rich bark, acacia gum and cinchona bark.

steps.reason: Tannins bind proteins and are astringent.
steps.result: Suitable for tanning leather and making dyes.
steps.predictPrompt: What can acacia gum be used for?

steps.reason: The gum swells in water and forms a sticky gel.
steps.result: Suitable as an adhesive, thickener or emulsifier.

steps.reason: It contains quinine, an alkaloid used against malaria.
steps.result: Valuable for medicine, but extraction and dose control are essential.

content.question: Why can a plant store toxic alkaloids without poisoning itself?
hints: Alkaloids are kept inside vacuoles or specialized ducts.
They are separated from the cytoplasm where most metabolism occurs.
The same compartmentation makes them available for defence when the plant is damaged.

lessons.title: Why Support and Movement?
lessons.objective: Explain why organisms need support and movement, and compare how plants and animals achieve both.

content.heading: Why support and movement?
paragraphs: A maize plant stands upright in the wind while a grasshopper beside it jumps out of reach. Both need support and movement, but they solve the problem with very different materials.

content.heading: Why support and movement matter
paragraphs: Support gives an organism shape and posture. It holds organs in place, keeps leaves facing light, anchors roots in soil and lets a body grow tall without collapsing under its own weight.

Movement lets an organism change position or move part of its body. Animals use it to find food, escape predators, seek mates and build shelters; plants move more slowly, growing towards resources or folding leaves when touched.

Support and movement are linked. A moving body needs a frame to pull against, and a frame needs muscles or turgor to move it. The two demands compete for materials and energy, so each organism strikes a different balance.
bullets: Support holds shape, organs and posture.
Movement finds food, escapes danger and reproduces.
A moving body needs a frame and a force to act on it.
content.takeaway: Support resists gravity; movement changes position.

check.question: Which statement best explains why support and movement are linked?
options: Support alone is enough for movement
A moving body needs a frame to pull against
Movement prevents an organism from growing
Support and movement use no energy
check.why: Muscles or turgor must act on a supporting frame to produce controlled movement.

content.heading: Plants: turgor and lignified walls
paragraphs: A herbaceous plant such as a young maize shoot is held up mainly by turgor. Water fills the vacuoles of parenchyma and collenchyma cells, pressing the cell walls outwards and keeping the stem firm.

Woody plants add lignified xylem and sclerenchyma fibres. These dead, rigid cells resist bending and compression, so a tree can carry a heavy canopy; the same tissues run through roots, stems and leaves.
Plant movement is usually slow growth or a reversible change in turgor. A shoot bends towards light as cells on one side elongate, and a Mimosa leaf folds within seconds when its pulvini lose water.
bullets: Turgor pressure supports young, soft stems.
Lignified xylem and sclerenchyma support woody plants.
Plant movement uses growth or reversible turgor changes.
content.takeaway: Plants stand on water pressure and lignified walls.

check.question: Which tissue keeps a young herbaceous stem firm?
check.why: Turgor pressure in living parenchyma and collenchyma cells keeps soft stems upright.

content.heading: Animals: skeletons and muscles
paragraphs: Animals use three main support systems. An earthworm has a hydrostatic skeleton, in which fluid under pressure in body segments works against circular and longitudinal muscles; an insect has a hard exoskeleton; a mammal has an internal endoskeleton of bone and cartilage.

Movement happens when muscles pull on the support. Muscles can contract and shorten but cannot push, so they work in antagonistic pairs across joints: one pulls a limb one way while the other pulls it back.

The choice of support carries trade-offs. A hydrostatic skeleton suits soft bodies and burrowing, an exoskeleton protects but must be moulted, and an endoskeleton grows with the body and allows large size at the cost of more internal tissue.
bullets: Hydrostatic skeleton: fluid pressure plus muscles.
Exoskeleton: external covering, must be moulted.
Endoskeleton: internal bone and cartilage, grows with the body.
content.takeaway: Every animal moves by pulling against a support.

check.question: Which support system must be shed for the animal to grow?
check.why: A rigid exoskeleton cannot expand, so arthropods moult and grow a new one.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Support holds shape and posture; movement changes position and uses energy. Plants use turgor and lignified walls, while animals use hydrostatic skeletons, exoskeletons or endoskeletons and pull with antagonistic muscles.

content.problem: An earthworm has no hard skeleton, yet it burrows; a grasshopper has a hard covering, yet it jumps. Compare how each combines support and movement.

steps.reason: Fluid in the coelom resists compression, and circular and longitudinal muscles change the body shape.
steps.result: A hydrostatic skeleton produces burrowing movement.
steps.predictPrompt: What supports the grasshopper instead?

steps.reason: Chitin forms a jointed exoskeleton outside the body.
steps.result: Muscles inside pull on the exoskeleton to move the legs.

steps.reason: The earthworm's soft body grows continuously, but chitin cannot stretch much.
steps.result: The grasshopper must moult to grow.

steps.reason: Both animals use muscles that pull against a support.
steps.result: Different materials, same principle of movement.

content.question: Why can a plant stand upright without a skeleton?
hints: Turgor pressure in living cells pushes the walls outward.
Lignified xylem and sclerenchyma resist bending in older parts.
When cells lose water, the plant wilts because that pressure falls.

lessons.title: Plant Movements and Tropisms
lessons.objective: Distinguish tropic, tactic and nastic movements, describe sleep movements, and explain the role of auxin in growth regions.

content.heading: Plant movements and tropisms
paragraphs: A sunflower turns towards the sun, a pond Euglena swims towards light, and a Mimosa leaf folds when touched. All three are plant-like movements, but they work in different ways.

content.heading: Tropisms: growth in a direction
paragraphs: A tropism is a growth response whose direction depends on the stimulus. Shoots usually show positive phototropism and negative geotropism, while roots show positive geotropism and negative phototropism; roots also grow towards water (hydrotropism) and tendrils curl around support (thigmotropism).

The response begins in the growing regions. At the shoot tip, the zone of cell division makes new cells, the zone of elongation lengthens them, and the zone of differentiation matures them; auxin, made at the tip, moves down and controls elongation.

In phototropism, auxin gathers on the shaded side of a shoot and makes those cells elongate more, so the shoot bends towards light. In a root, auxin gathers on the lower side and inhibits elongation there, so the root bends downwards.
bullets: Tropism: directional growth towards or away from a stimulus.
Shoot tip and root tip are the growth regions; auxin controls elongation.
Auxin promotes shoot elongation but inhibits root elongation at high levels.
content.takeaway: A tropism is growth bending towards or away from a stimulus.

check.question: A shoot bends towards light because auxin
options: Collects on the lit side and stops growth
Collects on the shaded side and increases elongation
Is destroyed by light on both sides
check.why: Auxin moves away from light, so shaded cells elongate more and the shoot bends towards the light.

content.heading: Tactic movements: the whole organism moves
paragraphs: A tactic movement is a movement of the whole organism or cell in response to a stimulus. Phototaxis is movement towards or away from light, chemotaxis is movement along a chemical gradient, and geotaxis is movement in response to gravity.

Euglena and Chlamydomonas swim towards light using their flagella, so photosynthesis can continue. Sperm cells swim towards chemicals released by the egg, and some bacteria move towards nutrients or away from toxins.

Tactic movements are usually fast and reversible, and they are common in small aquatic organisms that cannot grow towards a resource. The direction of movement is set by the stimulus, not by the direction of growth.
bullets: Taxis: whole organism moves towards or away from a stimulus.
Examples: phototaxis in Euglena, chemotaxis in sperm and bacteria.
Fast, reversible and common in small aquatic organisms.
content.takeaway: A taxis moves the whole organism; a tropism bends a growing part.

check.question: A sperm cell swimming towards the egg is an example of
check.why: The sperm follows a chemical gradient released by the egg, which is chemotaxis.

content.heading: Nastic movements and sleep
paragraphs: A nastic movement is a response to the intensity of a stimulus rather than its direction. The whole organ may fold, droop or open, and the movement is reversible because it depends on turgor rather than growth.

Seismonasty is the folding of Mimosa pudica leaves after touch or shaking; the pulvini at the leaf bases lose water and the leaflets collapse. Photonasty and thermonasty open and close petals in response to light and temperature.

Sleep movements, or nyctinasty, are the nightly folding of leaves in many legumes, such as tamarind and some beans. The leaves return to their daytime position when light returns, so the movement follows a daily rhythm rather than a permanent change in shape.
bullets: Nastic movement: non-directional, reversible, driven by turgor.
Seismonasty: Mimosa folds when touched.
Nyctinasty or sleep movement: leaves fold at night.
content.takeaway: Nastic movements answer how strong a stimulus is, not where it comes from.

check.question: The folding of Mimosa leaves after touch is called
check.why: Seismonasty is a reversible turgor response to touch or shaking.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Tropism = directional growth; taxis = whole-organism movement; nasty = non-directional turgor movement. Link auxin to shoot and root bending, and remember Mimosa pudica as the standard example of seismonasty.

content.problem: A bean seedling on a windowsill bends towards the window, while its roots grow downwards. Explain both responses using auxin.

steps.reason: Light comes mainly from one side.
steps.result: The shoot shows positive phototropism.
steps.predictPrompt: Where does auxin collect?

steps.operation: Place the auxin in the shoot
steps.reason: Auxin moves away from light to the shaded side.
steps.result: Shaded cells elongate more, so the shoot bends towards the window.

steps.reason: Gravity pulls auxin to the lower side of the root.
steps.result: High auxin inhibits root cell elongation, so the upper side grows faster and the root bends down.

steps.reason: The shoot is positively phototropic and negatively geotropic; the root is positively geotropic.
steps.result: One hormone, two opposite growth effects depending on the organ.

content.question: Why does a Mimosa leaf fold quickly when touched, but a sunflower does not?
hints: Mimosa uses turgor changes in pulvini, not growth.
The response is reversible and can repeat.
A sunflower's phototropism depends on differential growth, which is slower.

lessons.title: Supporting Tissues in Animals
lessons.objective: Relate the location and structure of chitin, cartilage and bone to their supporting functions.

content.heading: Supporting tissues in animals
paragraphs: A grasshopper's armour, a cow's ear and a goat's thigh bone all support the body, yet one is flexible, one springs back, and one is rigid. Their materials explain the difference.

content.heading: Chitin: support outside the body
paragraphs: Chitin is a tough, lightweight polysaccharide containing nitrogen. It forms the exoskeleton of insects, crabs, prawns and other arthropods, and is also found in the cell walls of fungi.

The chitin covering protects the body, resists water loss and gives a surface for muscles to pull against. In insects it is divided into plates and jointed sections, so the animal can move while still being supported.

Chitin cannot stretch much, so an arthropod must moult to grow. The old exoskeleton splits and is shed, and a new, soft one expands before it hardens; this leaves the animal vulnerable until hardening is complete.
bullets: Chitin: nitrogen-containing polysaccharide, tough and waterproof.
Forms the jointed exoskeleton of arthropods.
Must be moulted for growth; the soft new shell is vulnerable.
content.takeaway: Chitin supports from outside but must be shed to grow.

check.question: Arthropods must moult because chitin
options: Cannot stretch enough to allow growth
check.why: The rigid exoskeleton cannot expand, so it is shed and replaced as the animal grows.

content.heading: Cartilage: flexible support
paragraphs: Cartilage is a firm but flexible tissue made of collagen fibres in a gel-like matrix. Its cells, chondrocytes, sit in small spaces called lacunae, and the tissue has no blood vessels, so it heals slowly.
Cartilage is found in the pinna of the ear, the tip of the nose, the trachea, the intervertebral discs and the ends of long bones. In each place it supports without making the part rigid.

At joints, articular cartilage covers the bone ends, reduces friction and absorbs shock. In the trachea, C-shaped cartilage rings keep the airway open; in the ear, flexible cartilage bends without breaking.
bullets: Cartilage: flexible, avascular, chondrocytes in lacunae.
Locations: ear, nose, trachea, discs and bone ends.
Functions: support, shock absorption and low-friction surfaces.
content.takeaway: Cartilage supports where the body must bend or absorb shock.

check.question: Which property of cartilage makes it suitable for the tip of the nose?
options: It is flexible and springs back
It has a rich blood supply
check.why: Flexible cartilage bends under pressure and returns to shape without breaking.

content.heading: Bone: rigid living support
paragraphs: Bone is a living tissue with a matrix of collagen fibres and calcium phosphate. Osteocytes lie in lacunae, and blood vessels run through channels, so the tissue can grow and repair.
Compact bone forms the hard outer layer, while spongy bone inside is lighter and has a network of struts. The periosteum covers the outside, and red marrow in spongy bone makes blood cells.

Bones form the endoskeleton, protect organs, store calcium and phosphate, and give muscles a place to attach. Their rigidity supports the body, while their joints allow movement; bone is therefore both a frame and a mineral bank.
bullets: Bone: collagen and calcium phosphate matrix, living cells.
Compact bone is hard; spongy bone is light and holds marrow.
Functions: support, protection, attachment, mineral store and blood cell production.
content.takeaway: Bone is a living frame that also stores minerals.

check.question: The hardness of bone comes mainly from
check.why: Mineral salts, mainly calcium phosphate, harden the collagen framework of bone.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Chitin is outside and must be moulted; cartilage is flexible and avascular; bone is rigid, vascular and living. Match each material to its location: arthropod covering, ear or joint, and skeleton.

content.problem: A student compares a crab's shell, a shark's skeleton and a cow's thigh bone. Identify the supporting material in each and one consequence.

steps.reason: It is a hard external covering made of chitin.
steps.result: An exoskeleton that protects but must be moulted.
steps.predictPrompt: What supports the shark?

steps.reason: The skeleton is made of cartilage, not bone.
steps.result: A flexible endoskeleton that grows with the body.

steps.reason: Bone contains calcium phosphate and collagen.
steps.result: A rigid endoskeleton that supports weight and stores minerals.

steps.reason: Each material sits in a different place and does a different job.
steps.result: Chitin covers, cartilage flexes, and bone bears load.

content.question: Why is cartilage better than bone for the ends of long bones?
hints: It is smooth and reduces friction at the joint.
It absorbs shock during movement.
It has no blood vessels, so it heals slowly, but it suits a moving surface.

lessons.title: Skeletons and Their Functions
lessons.objective: Distinguish exoskeletons, endoskeletons and hydrostatic skeletons, and relate the mammalian skeleton's layout to support, protection, movement and breathing.

content.heading: Skeletons and their functions
paragraphs: A beetle's shell, an earthworm's fluid-filled body and a footballer's rib cage all support and protect, but only one is a true skeleton of bone. The differences shape how each animal moves and grows.

content.heading: Exoskeleton, endoskeleton and hydrostatic skeleton
paragraphs: An exoskeleton lies outside the body. Arthropods use chitin, and some molluscs use calcium carbonate shells; the covering protects the body and gives muscles a surface to pull against, but it must be moulted or added to as the animal grows.

An endoskeleton lies inside the body. Vertebrates use bone and cartilage, and the skeleton grows with the animal, supports a large body and protects internal organs; muscles attach to the outside of the bones.

A hydrostatic skeleton uses fluid under pressure, as in earthworms and jellyfish. Muscles change the shape of the fluid-filled body, producing movement without hard parts; this suits soft-bodied animals but cannot support great weight on land.
bullets: Exoskeleton: outside, protective, must be moulted.
Endoskeleton: inside, grows with the body, allows large size.
Hydrostatic skeleton: fluid pressure and muscles, no hard parts.
content.takeaway: Where the skeleton sits decides how the animal grows and moves.

check.question: Which skeleton grows with the animal without moulting?
check.why: An internal endoskeleton enlarges as the animal grows and does not need to be shed.

content.heading: The mammalian skeleton layout
paragraphs: The mammalian skeleton is divided into the axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton. The axial skeleton includes the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum; the appendicular skeleton includes the pectoral girdle, pelvic girdle and limbs.

An adult human has about 206 bones, joined at joints and held by ligaments. The skull protects the brain, the vertebral column supports the trunk and protects the spinal cord, and the rib cage surrounds the heart and lungs.

The limbs are built as levers: the humerus, radius and ulna in the arm, and the femur, tibia and fibula in the leg. Girdles attach the limbs to the axial skeleton, so body weight is transferred to the legs during standing and walking.
bullets: Axial: skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum.
Appendicular: girdles and limbs.
About 206 bones in an adult human, linked by joints and ligaments.
content.takeaway: Axial protects the core; appendicular moves the body.

check.question: Which group belongs to the axial skeleton?
check.why: The axial skeleton forms the central axis and includes the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum.

content.heading: Support, protection, movement and breathing
paragraphs: Support: the skeleton holds the body upright, gives it shape and anchors soft organs. Protection: the skull, rib cage and vertebral column shield the brain, heart, lungs and spinal cord.

Movement: muscles attach to bones by tendons, and bones act as levers at joints, so a small muscle contraction can move a limb. Respiration: the ribs and sternum move with the diaphragm, changing the volume of the thorax and drawing air in or out.

Bones also store calcium and phosphate and house marrow that makes blood cells. These functions explain why a broken rib can affect breathing and why a broken long bone can disturb the whole body, not just the limb.
bullets: Support and protection of organs.
Movement through muscles, tendons and joints.
Breathing through rib movement; mineral storage and blood cell production.
content.takeaway: The skeleton is a frame, shield, lever and pump handle.

check.question: The skeleton helps breathing mainly by
options: Moving the ribs and sternum to change thorax volume
check.why: Rib and sternum movements, with the diaphragm, change thoracic volume and move air.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Exoskeleton outside, endoskeleton inside, hydrostatic skeleton from fluid pressure. For mammals, link axial bones to protection and the rib cage to breathing, not just movement; the same skeleton also stores minerals.

content.problem: A footballer breaks a rib and later a leg bone. Explain how each injury affects a different function of the skeleton.

steps.reason: Ribs protect the lungs and move during breathing.
steps.result: A broken rib can make breathing painful and reduce ventilation.
steps.predictPrompt: What does the leg bone do?

steps.reason: The femur supports weight and acts as a lever for walking.
steps.result: A broken femur affects support and movement.

steps.reason: Protection, support, movement and breathing are separate but connected functions.
steps.result: The same skeleton serves all four, so the effect depends on which bone is damaged.

content.question: Why can an insect not simply grow larger inside its exoskeleton?
hints: Chitin is rigid and cannot stretch much.
The old shell must be shed and a new one expanded.
Moulting leaves the insect soft and vulnerable, so it must hide.

lessons.title: Joints and Movement
lessons.objective: Differentiate fibrous, cartilaginous and synovial joints, describe synovial joint structure, and explain antagonistic muscle action.

content.heading: Joints and movement
paragraphs: A goalkeeper's shoulder rotates, a runner's knee bends and the bones of the skull stay locked together. The type of joint decides how much movement is possible.

content.heading: Three classes of joint
paragraphs: A joint is a place where two or more bones meet. Fibrous joints, such as the sutures of the skull, are held by tough fibres and allow no movement; cartilaginous joints, such as those between vertebrae, allow slight movement.
Synovial joints are freely movable. They have a cavity between the bone ends, filled with synovial fluid, and are the joints used in walking, throwing and writing.

The amount of movement depends on the tissue between the bones: dense fibres lock, cartilage allows a little, and a fluid-filled cavity allows a lot. Injury to any of these tissues can limit movement.
bullets: Fibrous: immovable, e.g. skull sutures.
Cartilaginous: slightly movable, e.g. between vertebrae.
Synovial: freely movable, e.g. knee, shoulder and elbow.
content.takeaway: The joint's tissue sets how far the bones can move.

check.question: Which joint type allows the greatest movement?
check.why: A synovial joint has a fluid-filled cavity that allows free movement.

content.heading: Inside a synovial joint
paragraphs: The ends of the bones are covered by articular cartilage, which reduces friction and absorbs shock. A synovial membrane lines the capsule and secretes synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint and nourishes the cartilage.

Ligaments hold bone to bone and keep the joint stable, while tendons attach muscle to bone and transmit the pull. A joint capsule encloses the cavity, and bursae are small fluid-filled sacs that reduce friction where tendons rub.

Synovial joints come in shapes that suit their work: hinge joints at the elbow and knee, ball-and-socket joints at the shoulder and hip, pivot joints between the atlas and axis, and gliding joints between the carpals and tarsals.
bullets: Cartilage reduces friction; synovial fluid lubricates.
Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone.
Hinge, ball-and-socket, pivot and gliding joints suit different movements.
content.takeaway: Cartilage, fluid, ligaments and tendons make a joint work.

check.question: Which structure attaches a muscle to a bone?
check.why: A tendon attaches skeletal muscle to bone and transmits the muscle's pull.

content.heading: Muscles pull in pairs
paragraphs: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tendons. When a muscle contracts, it shortens and pulls the bone; it cannot push, so movement in the opposite direction needs another muscle.

At the elbow, the biceps contracts to flex the joint and the triceps contracts to extend it. These antagonistic muscles work in pairs: while one contracts, the other relaxes, and the joint moves smoothly.

The bone acts as a lever, the joint as the fulcrum and the muscle as the effort. Nerve impulses trigger contraction, and ATP supplies the energy; without either, the joint may be stable but cannot move.
bullets: Muscles contract and pull; they never push.
Antagonistic pairs move a joint in opposite directions.
