Bone = lever, joint = fulcrum, muscle = effort.
content.takeaway: Joints direct movement; antagonistic muscles provide the pull.

check.question: The biceps and triceps at the elbow are described as antagonistic because they
options: Pull the joint in opposite directions
check.why: The biceps flexes and the triceps extends the elbow, so their pulls oppose each other.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Fibrous joints do not move, cartilaginous joints move slightly, and synovial joints move freely. In a synovial joint, cartilage and fluid reduce friction; ligaments hold bones, tendons hold muscles, and bursae reduce rubbing.

content.problem: A patient cannot straighten the knee after an injury. Identify the joint type, the structures that may be damaged and the muscle that extends the knee.

steps.reason: The knee is a hinge synovial joint.
steps.result: It allows flexion and extension in one plane.
steps.predictPrompt: What structures stabilise it?

steps.reason: Ligaments hold bone to bone, and tendons attach muscles.
steps.result: Damage to the quadriceps tendon or patellar ligament can block extension.

steps.reason: The quadriceps on the front of the thigh straightens the knee.
steps.result: A weakened quadriceps or damaged tendon prevents extension.

steps.reason: The hamstrings flex the knee and are antagonistic to the quadriceps.
steps.result: Balanced pairs are needed for controlled movement.

content.question: Why does a footballer need both strong ligaments and strong muscles around the knee?
hints: Ligaments hold the bones together and limit unwanted movement.
Muscles produce the movement and absorb forces.
Cartilage and synovial fluid reduce friction but do not replace strength.

lessons.title: Asexual and Sexual Reproduction
lessons.objective: Differentiate asexual from sexual reproduction, and describe binary fission and budding with examples.

content.heading: Asexual and sexual reproduction
paragraphs: A Paramecium in a pond splits into two within an hour, while a goat must find a mate before it can produce a kid. The two routes to offspring could hardly be more different.

content.heading: Two routes to offspring
paragraphs: Asexual reproduction uses one parent. There are no gametes and no fertilisation, so the offspring are genetically identical to the parent and to one another; the process is usually fast and can produce many offspring.
Sexual reproduction uses two parents. Male and female gametes fuse at fertilisation, so each offspring receives a mixture of genes and differs from both parents and from its siblings.

Asexual reproduction suits stable environments where a successful parent can be copied, while sexual reproduction generates variation that may help a population survive disease or change. Many organisms can use both routes at different times.
bullets: Asexual: one parent, no gametes, identical offspring.
Sexual: two parents, gamete fusion, varied offspring.
Asexual is fast; sexual creates variation.
content.takeaway: Asexual copies; sexual mixes.

check.question: Which feature distinguishes sexual from asexual reproduction?
check.why: Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of male and female gametes, which asexual reproduction does not.

content.heading: Fission: one cell becomes two
paragraphs: Binary fission is the division of a single cell into two daughter cells. In Paramecium, the cell divides transversely; in Amoeba, the nucleus divides first and the cytoplasm then separates, producing two similar individuals.
The process is a form of mitosis, so each daughter receives a complete set of genes. Under good conditions, Paramecium can divide several times a day, and a small population can grow rapidly.
Bacteria also divide by binary fission, but they have no true nucleus. Fission is therefore a simple, efficient way for unicellular organisms to increase numbers without a mate.
bullets: Binary fission: one parent cell divides into two.
Paramecium divides transversely; Amoeba divides after nuclear division.
Mitosis gives each daughter a complete gene set.
content.takeaway: Fission copies one cell into two.

check.question: Binary fission in Paramecium is best described as
options: Transverse division of one cell into two
check.why: Paramecium divides across its body into two similar daughter cells.

content.heading: Budding: a new individual from a bud
paragraphs: In budding, a small outgrowth forms on the parent and develops into a new individual. The bud may detach or remain attached, so budding can produce a colony of identical individuals.
Yeast is a single-celled fungus that buds rapidly: the nucleus divides, one daughter nucleus moves into the bud, and the bud pinches off. Hydra, a freshwater cnidarian, also reproduces by budding.

Budding differs from fission because the parent keeps its original body and the new individual starts as a small outgrowth. Both processes are asexual, so both produce genetically identical offspring.
bullets: Budding: a small outgrowth becomes a new individual.
Yeast and Hydra are standard examples.
The bud may detach or stay attached as a colony.
content.takeaway: Budding grows a new individual from the parent's side.

check.question: Which organism is the standard example of budding?
check.why: Yeast reproduces asexually by forming buds that pinch off from the parent cell.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Asexual reproduction uses one parent and makes clones; sexual reproduction uses two parents and makes variation. Fission splits a cell into two; budding grows a new individual from an outgrowth.

content.problem: A student observes a Paramecium dividing across its middle and a yeast cell forming a small outgrowth. Identify each process and explain one consequence.

steps.reason: The cell divides transversely into two similar cells.
steps.result: Binary fission.
steps.predictPrompt: What is the yeast doing?

steps.reason: A small bud forms and receives a nucleus before pinching off.
steps.result: Budding.

steps.reason: Both processes are asexual and involve mitosis.
steps.result: The offspring are genetically identical to the parent.

steps.reason: Rapid asexual reproduction suits stable, favourable conditions.
steps.result: Populations can grow quickly without mates.

content.question: Why can a single Paramecium start a new population, while a goat cannot?
hints: Paramecium reproduces asexually by fission.
The goat needs a mate and gamete fusion.
Sexual reproduction creates variation but is slower.

lessons.title: Vegetative Propagation
lessons.objective: Describe natural and artificial vegetative propagation and apply the methods to crop production.

content.heading: Vegetative propagation
paragraphs: A farmer cuts a cassava stem into short pieces and plants them; months later each piece has become a new plant. No seed was involved.

content.heading: Natural vegetative propagation
paragraphs: Many plants reproduce without seeds using modified stems, roots or leaves. A runner is a stem that grows along the ground and roots at nodes, as in lawn grass; a rhizome is an underground stem, as in ginger and turmeric.

A tuber is a swollen underground stem with buds or 'eyes', as in yam and Irish potato; a bulb is a short underground stem surrounded by fleshy leaves, as in onion and garlic. Suckers are shoots that arise from the base of the parent, as in banana and plantain.
Each structure carries stored food and buds, so a new plant can grow when conditions are suitable. The offspring are identical to the parent, which is useful when the parent has desirable qualities.
bullets: Runners, rhizomes, tubers, bulbs and suckers are natural structures.
Examples: lawn grass, ginger, yam, onion and plantain.
Offspring are clones of the parent.
content.takeaway: Natural propagation uses the plant's own storage and buds.

check.question: Which structure is an underground stem with eyes?
check.why: A tuber such as yam or Irish potato is a swollen underground stem with buds called eyes.

content.heading: Artificial vegetative propagation
paragraphs: Farmers copy desirable plants using cuttings, layering, grafting, budding and tissue culture. A cutting is a piece of stem or root that is planted and grows into a new plant, as with cassava and sugar cane.

Layering roots a stem while it is still attached to the parent, then separates it; marcotting is a form of air layering used for guava and citrus. Grafting joins a scion to a rootstock, as in mango, citrus and rubber, while budding inserts a single bud into the rootstock.

Tissue culture grows many plantlets from small pieces of tissue in a sterile medium, and is used for banana and plantain. These methods avoid the uncertainty of seed germination and produce uniform plants.
bullets: Cuttings: cassava and sugar cane.
Layering and marcotting: guava and citrus.
Grafting and budding: mango, citrus and rubber; tissue culture: banana.
content.takeaway: Cuttings, layers, grafts and cultures copy a chosen plant.

check.question: Which method joins a scion to a rootstock?
check.why: Grafting attaches the scion of one plant to the rootstock of another so they grow as one.

content.heading: Why farmers use vegetative propagation
paragraphs: The main advantage is that the new plants are genetically identical to the parent, so a high-yielding, disease-resistant or tasty variety is preserved. Propagation is also faster than raising trees from seed, and it works for seedless plants such as banana.

The method has costs. Uniform plants may all be vulnerable to the same disease, and cuttings can carry viruses from the parent; some methods need skill, and grafted plants may fail if the scion and rootstock are incompatible.

In crop production, farmers match the method to the crop: yam setts, cassava stem cuttings, plantain suckers and grafted mango seedlings. Good planting material, clean tools and proper spacing improve success.
bullets: Advantages: true-to-type, fast and works for seedless plants.
Risks: uniform disease susceptibility and transmission of pathogens.
Match the method to the crop and use clean planting material.
content.takeaway: Vegetative propagation trades variation for a reliable copy.

check.question: One major risk of planting many cuttings from one parent is
check.why: Because the plants are clones, a disease that attacks one can attack all of them.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Natural propagation uses runners, rhizomes, tubers, bulbs and suckers; artificial propagation uses cuttings, layering, grafting, budding and tissue culture. The reward is uniform plants; the risk is uniform disease susceptibility.

content.problem: A farmer wants more plants from one outstanding mango tree and one cassava field. Choose a method for each and give one reason.

steps.reason: Mango is a tree, and seedlings vary from the parent.
steps.result: Grafting or budding onto a rootstock preserves the variety.
steps.predictPrompt: What about the cassava?

steps.reason: Cassava stem cuttings root easily and are cheap.
steps.result: Stem cuttings produce many identical plants.

steps.reason: All the new plants are clones.
steps.result: They may share the same disease weakness, so use clean stock and several varieties.

content.question: Why is vegetative propagation especially useful for banana and plantain?
hints: These crops are seedless or produce very few viable seeds.
Suckers and tissue culture give many identical plants.
Uniform plants are useful, but they need careful disease control.

lessons.title: Flower Structure and Pollination
lessons.objective: Relate floral parts to their functions, compare self- and cross-pollination, and explain the advantages of cross-pollination.

content.heading: Flower structure and pollination
paragraphs: A hibiscus flower opens with bright petals and a prominent stigma, while a maize tassel releases clouds of pollen into the wind. Both are built for pollination, but not for the same visitor.

content.heading: Parts of a flower
paragraphs: A flower sits on a receptacle. The sepals protect the bud, and the petals attract pollinators; together they form the calyx and corolla. Inside are the stamens, each with an anther on a filament, and the carpel or pistil.
The carpel has a stigma that receives pollen, a style through which the pollen tube grows, and an ovary containing ovules. The ovary later becomes the fruit, and the ovules become the seeds.

A bisexual flower has both stamens and carpels, while a unisexual flower has only one; maize and pawpaw have separate male and female flowers. The parts work together: attraction, pollen transfer and protection of the female gametes.
bullets: Sepals protect; petals attract pollinators.
Stamen: anther and filament, the male part.
Carpel: stigma, style and ovary, the female part.
content.takeaway: The flower is a reproductive shoot built for pollen transfer.

check.question: Which part of the carpel receives pollen?
check.why: The stigma is the sticky or feathery tip that receives pollen grains.

content.heading: Pollination and its agents
paragraphs: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma. Self-pollination happens within the same flower or plant, while cross-pollination happens between different plants of the same species.

Wind-pollinated flowers such as maize and grass have small petals, exposed anthers and feathery stigmas; they release large amounts of light pollen. Insect-pollinated flowers such as hibiscus and sunflower have bright petals, scent and nectar to attract visitors that carry pollen.

Water-pollinated plants such as Vallisneria release pollen that floats to the stigma, and some flowers are pollinated by birds or bats. The agent matters because it determines how much pollen is wasted and how far genes travel.
bullets: Pollination: pollen from anther to stigma.
Wind flowers: small petals, exposed anthers, feathery stigmas.
Insect flowers: colour, scent and nectar attract carriers.
content.takeaway: Pollination is a delivery service; the agent sets the route.

check.question: Which feature is typical of a wind-pollinated flower?
check.why: Wind-pollinated flowers expose their anthers and have feathery stigmas to catch airborne pollen.

content.heading: Why cross-pollination matters
paragraphs: Cross-pollination brings together gametes from different plants, so the offspring are genetically varied. Variation can help a population resist disease, adapt to changing conditions and produce hybrid vigour in the next generation.

The cost is that cross-pollination depends on an agent, so it can fail in wet, windy or pollinator-poor conditions. Self-pollination is more reliable and preserves a successful genotype, but it reduces variation and can concentrate harmful recessive traits.
Pollination is not fertilisation. Pollen still has to germinate and grow a tube to the ovule; if the pollen is incompatible or the tube fails, no seed forms even though pollination happened.
bullets: Cross-pollination increases genetic variation.
It depends on agents and can fail.
Pollination must be followed by fertilisation.
content.takeaway: Cross-pollination buys variation at the price of uncertainty.

check.question: One advantage of cross-pollination is that it
check.why: Mixing gametes from different plants produces offspring with new gene combinations.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Sepals protect, petals attract, stamens make pollen and the carpel receives it. Wind flowers are small and feathery; insect flowers are showy and scented. Cross-pollination increases variation but needs an agent.

content.problem: A farmer notices that maize plants at the edge of a field produce fewer grains than those in the middle. Suggest a reason and a solution.

steps.reason: Maize is wind-pollinated.
steps.result: Pollen must travel on the wind to the silks.
steps.predictPrompt: Why would edge plants receive less pollen?

steps.reason: Pollen concentration falls at the edge, and wind may carry it away.
steps.result: Fewer pollen grains land on the silks, so fewer ovules are fertilised.

steps.reason: Planting in blocks rather than long thin rows increases pollen availability.
steps.result: A block layout improves pollination and grain fill.

content.question: Why do insect-pollinated flowers usually have bright petals and nectar, while wind-pollinated flowers do not?
hints: Insects must be attracted from a distance.
Nectar is a reward for the visit.
Wind does not need to be attracted, so those parts would be wasted.

lessons.title: Fertilization and Seed Formation
lessons.objective: Describe pollination, pollen-tube growth and double fertilization, and explain how seeds and fruits form.

content.heading: Fertilization and seed formation
paragraphs: After a pollen grain lands on a hibiscus stigma, a tube grows down the style towards an ovule. A few days later, the flower's ovary is swelling into a fruit.

content.heading: From pollen grain to pollen tube
paragraphs: A pollen grain that lands on a compatible stigma absorbs water and germinates. It produces a pollen tube that grows down the style, guided by chemicals from the ovary, and enters the ovule through a small opening called the micropyle.
The pollen grain contains two male gametes. As the tube grows, they travel behind its tip; the tube nucleus directs growth while the gametes wait to be released into the embryo sac.
This journey is why pollination and fertilisation are separate events. Pollination only delivers the pollen; the tube must grow, and the gametes must fuse with the female cells inside the ovule.
bullets: Pollen germinates on the stigma and grows a tube.
The tube reaches the ovule through the micropyle.
Two male gametes travel inside the tube.
content.takeaway: Pollination delivers pollen; the pollen tube delivers gametes.

check.question: The pollen tube enters the ovule through the
check.why: The micropyle is the small opening in the ovule through which the pollen tube enters.

content.heading: Double fertilisation
paragraphs: Inside the embryo sac, one male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form the zygote, which develops into the embryo. The other male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei to form a triploid cell that becomes the endosperm.

This is double fertilisation, and it is characteristic of flowering plants. The zygote supplies the new plant, while the endosperm supplies stored food for the seedling; in some seeds the endosperm is used up as the cotyledons grow.
After fertilisation, the ovule becomes the seed, its integuments become the seed coat, and the ovary wall becomes the fruit wall or pericarp. The flower's petals, stamens and style usually wither.
bullets: One gamete + egg = zygote (embryo).
One gamete + two polar nuclei = endosperm.
Ovule becomes seed; ovary becomes fruit.
content.takeaway: Double fertilisation makes an embryo and its food supply.

check.question: Double fertilisation in flowering plants produces
check.why: One fusion forms the zygote and the other forms the endosperm, hence 'double' fertilisation.

content.heading: What happens after fertilisation
paragraphs: The ovary grows as the fruit develops, protected by hormones such as auxin and gibberellin. The fruit wall may become fleshy or dry, and the seed inside contains the embryo and a food store.

If fertilisation fails, the flower may drop without forming a fruit. Some fruits develop without fertilisation, a condition called parthenocarpy, and these seedless fruits can be induced with plant hormones.
The seed is the link to the next generation: it protects the embryo, stores food and waits for suitable conditions to germinate. The fruit adds another layer of protection and often helps dispersal.
bullets: Fruit develops from the ovary; seed develops from the ovule.
Failed fertilisation usually means no fruit.
Parthenocarpy produces seedless fruit without fertilisation.
content.takeaway: Fertilisation switches the flower from attraction to seed production.

check.question: The fruit wall develops from the
check.why: The ovary wall becomes the pericarp, or fruit wall, after fertilisation.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Pollination is pollen transfer; fertilisation is gamete fusion. In flowering plants, double fertilisation gives a zygote and an endosperm. The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

content.problem: A gardener pollinates a flower by hand, but no fruit forms. Suggest two possible reasons.

steps.reason: Pollen must be compatible with the stigma and style.
steps.result: Incompatible pollen may fail to germinate or the tube may stop growing.
steps.predictPrompt: What else could fail?

steps.reason: The tube must reach the ovule through the style and micropyle.
steps.result: Damage or poor conditions can stop the tube.

steps.reason: Gametes must fuse to form a zygote and endosperm.
steps.result: Without double fertilisation, the ovary may drop instead of forming fruit.

content.question: Why is double fertilisation described as 'double'?
hints: Two male gametes are involved.
One fuses with the egg, the other with two polar nuclei.
The result is a zygote and an endosperm.

lessons.title: Fruits, Placentation and Dispersal
lessons.objective: Relate placentation types to fruit structure, distinguish simple, aggregate and multiple fruits, and explain seed dispersal.

content.heading: Fruits, placentation and dispersal
paragraphs: A pawpaw fruit is cut open to reveal seeds attached in rows, while a pineapple is formed from many flowers fused together. The arrangement of ovules and flowers decides what the fruit looks like.

content.heading: Placentation: where ovules attach
paragraphs: Placentation is the arrangement of ovules on the ovary wall. In marginal placentation, ovules sit along one suture, as in pea and bean; in axile placentation, they attach to a central axis in a divided ovary, as in tomato, citrus and hibiscus.

Parietal placentation places ovules on the outer wall, as in pawpaw and watermelon; free-central placentation has ovules on a central column without dividing walls, as in carnation; basal placentation has a single ovule at the base, as in sunflower and maize.
The arrangement affects how many seeds a fruit can hold and how they are packed. It also helps identify a plant from a cross-section of its ovary or fruit.
bullets: Marginal: pea and bean.
Axile: tomato, citrus and hibiscus; parietal: pawpaw and watermelon.
Free-central: carnation; basal: sunflower and maize.
content.takeaway: Placentation is the map of ovules inside the ovary.

check.question: Tomato seeds are attached to a central axis in a divided ovary. This is
check.why: Axile placentation places ovules on a central axis in an ovary divided into locules.

content.heading: Simple, aggregate and multiple fruits
paragraphs: A simple fruit develops from one ovary of one flower. It may be dry, such as a bean pod or maize grain, or succulent, such as tomato, orange and pawpaw.

An aggregate fruit develops from many separate carpels of one flower, as in raspberry and blackberry; each carpel forms a small fruitlet on a shared receptacle. A multiple fruit develops from the ovaries of many flowers in an inflorescence, as in pineapple, breadfruit and jackfruit.
Some fruits are false fruits because parts other than the ovary, such as the receptacle, become fleshy; apple, cashew and strawberry are examples. True fruits develop mainly from the ovary wall.
bullets: Simple fruit: one ovary, e.g. bean, tomato, orange.
Aggregate fruit: many carpels of one flower, e.g. raspberry.
Multiple fruit: many flowers, e.g. pineapple and breadfruit.
content.takeaway: Count the ovaries and flowers to name the fruit.

check.question: Pineapple is a multiple fruit because it develops from
check.why: A multiple fruit forms from the fused ovaries of many flowers in one inflorescence.

content.heading: Seed dispersal
paragraphs: Dispersal moves seeds away from the parent, reducing competition for light, water and nutrients and allowing the species to colonise new areas. Wind-dispersed seeds are light and may have wings or hairs, as in dandelion and silk cotton.

Water-dispersed seeds are buoyant and waterproof, as in coconut and water lily; animal-dispersed seeds may be fleshy and eaten, or have hooks that cling to fur, as in mango and Desmodium. Some fruits burst open explosively, as in bean and castor.
The fruit's structure matches its dispersal agent. A fleshy fruit attracts animals, a winged fruit catches wind, and a hooked fruit hitchhikes; the seed inside is protected until it lands.
bullets: Wind: light, winged or hairy seeds.
Water: buoyant, waterproof seeds such as coconut.
Animals: fleshy or hooked fruits; some fruits burst open.
content.takeaway: The fruit's design tells you how its seeds travel.

check.question: A seed with hooks is most likely dispersed by
check.why: Hooks cling to animal fur or feathers, so the seed is carried away.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Placentation places ovules: marginal, axile, parietal, free-central or basal. Fruit type depends on the ovary and flower: simple, aggregate or multiple. Dispersal agents match fruit design and protect the seeds.

content.problem: A fruit has a single ovary, fleshy tissue and small hard seeds. Suggest its fruit type, one likely dispersal agent and one advantage of that dispersal.

steps.reason: One ovary makes it a simple fruit.
steps.result: A simple succulent fruit.
steps.predictPrompt: How might the seeds travel?

steps.reason: Fleshy tissue attracts animals that eat the fruit.
steps.result: Animal dispersal.

steps.reason: Animals carry seeds away from the parent.
steps.result: Reduced competition and colonisation of new areas.

content.question: Why does a pea pod have seeds in a row along one side, while a tomato has seeds on a central axis?
hints: The two ovaries have different placentation.
Pea has marginal placentation along one suture.
Tomato has axile placentation on a central axis.

lessons.title: Mammalian Reproductive Systems
lessons.objective: Differentiate the male and female reproductive organs, relate their structures to gamete production, and outline the menstrual cycle.

content.heading: Mammalian reproductive systems
paragraphs: A bull and a cow, a man and a woman: each pair has different reproductive organs, but both are built to produce gametes and bring them together.

content.heading: The male system
paragraphs: The male reproductive system includes a pair of testes in the scrotum, a system of ducts and accessory glands. The testes contain seminiferous tubules where sperm are made and interstitial cells that secrete testosterone.

Sperm travel from the testis to the epididymis, where they mature, then through the vas deferens to the urethra. The seminal vesicles, prostate gland and Cowper's glands add fluid that nourishes and transports sperm, forming semen.
The scrotum keeps the testes slightly cooler than the body, which is necessary for sperm production. The penis delivers semen into the female vagina during intercourse.
bullets: Testes: sperm and testosterone.
Epididymis, vas deferens and urethra form the duct.
Seminal vesicles, prostate and Cowper's glands make semen.
content.takeaway: Testes make sperm; glands make the fluid that carries them.

check.question: Which gland secretes fluid that forms part of semen?
check.why: The prostate gland adds fluid to sperm, helping to form semen.

content.heading: The female system
paragraphs: The female system includes a pair of ovaries, fallopian tubes, the uterus, cervix and vagina. The ovaries produce ova and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone; the fallopian tube carries the egg towards the uterus.

The uterus has a thick muscular wall and a lining, the endometrium, where a fertilised egg can implant. The cervix is the narrow neck of the uterus, and the vagina is the muscular canal that receives the penis and serves as the birth canal.
At ovulation, a mature follicle releases an egg. If it is not fertilised, the lining is shed during menstruation; if it is fertilised, the lining is maintained for pregnancy.
bullets: Ovaries: ova, oestrogen and progesterone.
Fallopian tube: site of fertilisation.
Uterus: implantation and pregnancy; vagina: birth canal.
content.takeaway: Ovaries release eggs; the uterus shelters a pregnancy.

check.question: Fertilisation normally occurs in the
check.why: Sperm usually meet the egg in the fallopian tube, where fertilisation takes place.

content.heading: The menstrual cycle
paragraphs: The menstrual cycle is a monthly sequence of changes in the ovary and uterus. FSH from the pituitary stimulates a follicle to mature, and the follicle secretes oestrogen, which thickens the endometrium.
A surge of LH triggers ovulation around the middle of the cycle. The remains of the follicle become the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone and maintains the endometrium.

If fertilisation does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and the endometrium is shed as menstruation. If fertilisation occurs, the corpus luteum persists and supports early pregnancy until the placenta takes over.
bullets: FSH matures the follicle; oestrogen thickens the uterus lining.
LH surge triggers ovulation.
Progesterone maintains the lining; falling levels cause menstruation.
content.takeaway: Hormones build, release and shed the uterine lining.

check.question: Ovulation is triggered by a surge of
check.why: A sharp rise in luteinising hormone triggers the mature follicle to release its egg.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Testes produce sperm and testosterone; ovaries produce eggs, oestrogen and progesterone. Fertilisation occurs in the fallopian tube. FSH matures the follicle, LH triggers ovulation and progesterone maintains the lining during each cycle.

content.problem: A woman's blood test shows a high LH level and a mature follicle. Predict what will happen next and explain the hormone changes.

steps.reason: A surge of LH triggers ovulation.
steps.result: The follicle will release an egg.
steps.predictPrompt: What happens to the follicle after ovulation?

steps.reason: The ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum.
steps.result: It secretes progesterone.

steps.reason: Progesterone maintains the endometrium.
steps.result: The lining stays thick for possible implantation.

steps.reason: The corpus luteum degenerates if no embryo implants.
steps.result: Progesterone falls and menstruation follows.

content.question: Why does the uterus lining break down if the egg is not fertilised?
hints: The corpus luteum needs a signal from an implanting embryo to persist.
Without that signal, progesterone falls.
Low progesterone cannot maintain the endometrium, so it is shed.

lessons.title: Pregnancy and Birth
lessons.objective: Describe fertilization, implantation, placental exchange, gestation and birth, and explain how maternal health and nutrition affect the fetus.

content.heading: Pregnancy and birth
paragraphs: A fertilised egg divides as it travels down the fallopian tube, then settles into the uterus. Nine months later, contractions push a baby into the world.

content.heading: Fertilisation and implantation
paragraphs: Fertilisation happens in the fallopian tube, when one sperm penetrates the egg and their nuclei fuse. The resulting zygote divides repeatedly as it moves towards the uterus, forming a ball of cells called a blastocyst.

The blastocyst implants in the endometrium, where it is nourished at first by the uterine lining. The corpus luteum continues to secrete progesterone, preventing menstruation and maintaining the pregnancy.
The placenta develops from fetal and maternal tissues and becomes the exchange organ between mother and fetus. The umbilical cord connects the fetus to the placenta, carrying blood to and from it.
bullets: Fertilisation: fallopian tube; one sperm fuses with the egg.
Zygote divides and implants in the endometrium.
Placenta and umbilical cord connect fetus and mother.
content.takeaway: Fertilisation makes the zygote; implantation starts the pregnancy.

check.question: Implantation occurs when the blastocyst attaches to the
check.why: The blastocyst embeds in the endometrium, the lining of the uterus.

content.heading: The placenta and gestation
paragraphs: The placenta lets oxygen and nutrients pass from the mother's blood to the fetus, and carbon (IV) oxide and urea pass back. The two blood supplies are separated by a thin membrane, so they do not mix directly.

Gestation in humans lasts about nine months, or 38-40 weeks. The fetus grows and its organs mature; the amniotic fluid cushions it, and the placenta secretes hormones such as hCG, progesterone and oestrogen.

The mother's health and nutrition affect the fetus. A balanced diet with folic acid, iron, calcium and protein supports growth, while alcohol, smoking and some infections can harm the baby; antenatal care monitors blood pressure, anaemia and fetal growth.
bullets: Placenta: exchanges oxygen, nutrients and wastes.
Gestation: about 38-40 weeks in humans.
Maternal diet, folic acid and antenatal care protect the fetus.
content.takeaway: The placenta feeds and cleans the fetus; the mother's health supplies it.

check.question: Which substance passes from the fetus to the mother across the placenta?
check.why: Carbon (IV) oxide is a waste product that passes from fetal blood to maternal blood for excretion.

content.heading: Labour, birth and lactation
paragraphs: Labour begins when the uterus contracts rhythmically and the cervix dilates. Oxytocin stimulates stronger contractions, and the baby is pushed through the vagina; the placenta is delivered afterwards as the afterbirth.

Breastfeeding provides colostrum, which is rich in antibodies, and then milk with the right balance of nutrients. Suckling stimulates oxytocin release, which helps milk ejection and uterine contraction.
The mother needs rest, iron and a good diet after birth, and the baby needs warmth, feeding and immunisation. Complications such as heavy bleeding or infection require prompt medical care.
bullets: Labour: uterine contractions and cervical dilation deliver the baby.
Oxytocin drives contractions and milk ejection.
Colostrum provides antibodies; postnatal care supports mother and baby.
content.takeaway: Oxytocin drives birth and breastfeeding; the placenta follows the baby.

check.question: The first milk, rich in antibodies, is called
check.why: Colostrum is the antibody-rich first milk produced before mature breast milk.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Fertilisation in the fallopian tube, implantation in the endometrium, exchange in the placenta. Human gestation is about 38-40 weeks. Oxytocin drives labour and milk ejection; colostrum carries antibodies for the newborn.

content.problem: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with severe anaemia. Explain how this could affect the fetus and what care is needed.

steps.reason: Anaemia reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the mother's blood.
steps.result: Less oxygen reaches the placenta and fetus.
steps.predictPrompt: What might happen to fetal growth?

steps.reason: The fetus needs oxygen for growth and development.
steps.result: Growth may be slowed and the baby may be born underweight.

steps.reason: Iron supplements, a balanced diet and antenatal monitoring can correct anaemia.
steps.result: Treating the mother protects both her and the fetus.

content.question: Why is the placenta described as an exchange organ rather than a mixer of blood?
hints: Maternal and fetal blood are separated by a thin membrane.
Oxygen and nutrients diffuse across, but cells do not.
This separation protects the fetus from some harmful substances and immune reactions.

lessons.title: Reproductive Health and Contraception
lessons.objective: Explain modern methods of regulating reproduction and their role in family and reproductive health.

content.heading: Reproductive health and contraception
paragraphs: A young couple wants to delay their first child, while a mother of three wants to space her next pregnancy. Both are regulating reproduction, and both need accurate information.

content.heading: Why regulate reproduction
paragraphs: Family planning is the deliberate control of the number and spacing of children. It protects the mother's health, gives families time to recover and supports the care and education of each child.

Reproductive health means people can have safe, satisfying sexual lives, decide whether and when to have children, and be free from disease and coercion. Birth spacing reduces the risks of anaemia, premature birth and maternal death.
Regulation is not only about preventing pregnancy. It includes helping couples conceive when they want a child, preventing sexually transmitted infections and supporting maternal and child health.
bullets: Family planning controls the number and spacing of children.
Reproductive health includes choice, safety and disease prevention.
Birth spacing protects mother and child.
content.takeaway: Family planning is about choice, timing and health.

check.question: Birth spacing mainly helps to
check.why: Spacing pregnancies gives the mother time to recover and supports healthier outcomes for mother and child.

content.heading: Modern contraceptive methods
paragraphs: Barrier methods stop sperm meeting the egg; condoms also protect against sexually transmitted infections. Hormonal methods, such as pills, injectables and implants, prevent ovulation or thicken cervical mucus, and emergency pills reduce the chance of pregnancy after unprotected sex.

Intrauterine devices (IUDs) are placed in the uterus and may release copper or hormone. Surgical methods are permanent: tubal ligation blocks the fallopian tubes, while vasectomy cuts or blocks the vas deferens; both are for people who have completed their families.

Natural methods, such as the rhythm method and withdrawal, need no drugs but are less reliable. No method is perfect, and only condoms also protect against HIV and other STIs; a health worker can help choose the safest option.
bullets: Barrier: condoms, which also protect against STIs.
Hormonal: pills, injectables, implants and emergency pills.
IUDs and surgical methods; natural methods are less reliable.
content.takeaway: Match the method to health needs, not just convenience.

check.question: Which contraceptive method also protects against HIV and other STIs?
check.why: Condoms are a barrier that reduces the exchange of body fluids, so they also reduce STI transmission.

content.heading: Reproductive health and STIs
paragraphs: Sexually transmitted infections include gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydia, herpes and HIV/AIDS. Many are silent at first, so testing and early treatment matter; untreated infections can cause infertility, ectopic pregnancy and harm to a baby.

Prevention includes correct condom use, mutual fidelity, testing and avoiding shared needles. Vaccines protect against some infections, such as hepatitis B and HPV, and prompt treatment cures several bacterial STIs.

Reproductive health services also support infertility care and assisted reproduction such as IVF, and they counsel survivors of sexual violence. Accurate information, consent and access to care are part of the same package.
bullets: STIs include gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydia, herpes and HIV.
Condoms, testing, fidelity and vaccines reduce risk.
Untreated STIs can cause infertility and pregnancy complications.
content.takeaway: Prevention and early treatment protect fertility and life.

check.question: Which practice best reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections?
check.why: Correct condom use reduces the exchange of fluids that carry many STI pathogens.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Family planning spaces births; condoms are the common method that also blocks STIs. Hormonal, barrier, IUD and surgical methods suit different needs. Testing and early treatment protect fertility and save lives.

content.problem: A couple wants to delay pregnancy for two years and also reduce their risk of HIV. Recommend a method and explain the choice.

steps.reason: They need contraception and infection protection.
steps.result: A method that does both is ideal.
steps.predictPrompt: Which method does both?

steps.reason: Condoms are a barrier to sperm and to many pathogens.
steps.result: Correct and consistent condom use.
steps.predictPrompt: What if they also want a hormonal method?

steps.reason: Condoms can be used with a hormonal method for extra protection.
steps.result: Dual protection covers pregnancy and STIs.

content.question: Why is 'no method is 100% effective' an important message in family planning?
hints: Method failure and incorrect use can happen.
Condoms can break or be used inconsistently.
Emergency contraception and follow-up care matter when protection fails.

lessons.title: Meaning and Measurement of Growth
lessons.objective: Define growth, distinguish it from development, and describe how growth is measured and where it occurs in plants and animals.

content.heading: Meaning and measurement of growth
paragraphs: A maize seedling doubles its height in a week, while a lizard hatchling grows slowly to adult size. Both are growing, but the pattern and the measurement differ.

content.heading: What growth means
paragraphs: Growth is an irreversible increase in the size, mass or number of cells of an organism. It happens when cells divide, then enlarge and add new material, so the change cannot simply be reversed by losing water.

Growth is not the same as development. Development is the process by which cells and tissues become specialised and the organism matures, such as a seedling forming flowers or a child reaching puberty; an organism can grow without developing a new organ.
In practice, growth is shown by height, fresh mass, dry mass or cell number. Dry mass is the most reliable measure because it excludes the water that makes fresh mass fluctuate during the day.
bullets: Growth: irreversible increase in size, mass or cell number.
Development: specialisation and maturation of cells and organs.
Dry mass is the best measure because it ignores water changes.
content.takeaway: Growth adds matter; development adds function.

check.question: Which measurement best shows true growth without the effect of water uptake?
check.why: Dry mass measures the actual new material added, while fresh mass changes with water content.

content.heading: How growth is measured
paragraphs: A single measurement says little, so growth is followed over time. Height or length is easy to measure in plants and young animals, while mass is measured with a balance and cell number with a microscope.

When growth is plotted against time, many organisms show a sigmoid or S-shaped curve. A slow lag phase is followed by a rapid exponential phase, then a stationary phase as growth slows and the organism reaches maturity.

The curve helps compare treatments. A fertiliser that raises the exponential phase produces taller plants, while a disease that lengthens the lag phase delays establishment even if the final height is similar.
bullets: Take repeated measurements over time, not a single reading.
A sigmoid curve has lag, exponential and stationary phases.
Height, mass and cell counts reveal different aspects of growth.
content.takeaway: Growth is a curve, not a single measurement.

check.question: The rapid phase of a sigmoid growth curve is called the
check.why: During the exponential phase, cells divide and enlarge rapidly, so size or mass increases quickly.

content.heading: Where growth happens
paragraphs: Plants grow mainly at meristems. Apical meristems at the tips of roots and shoots add length, while lateral meristems such as the cambium add girth; this is why a plant can keep growing throughout its life.

Animals usually grow throughout the body and stop at adult size, although some organs and tissues continue to replace cells. Insects grow in bursts, shedding the exoskeleton at each moult, while mammals grow more continuously.
Growth depends on food, oxygen, water, suitable temperature and hormones. A lack of any one factor slows the curve, which is why nutrition and health during childhood affect final adult size.
bullets: Plants: apical meristems add length; lateral meristems add girth.
Animals: growth is more general and usually stops at adult size.
Food, oxygen, water, temperature and hormones control growth.
content.takeaway: Plants grow at tips and rings; animals grow all over.

check.question: Which tissue allows a plant to grow longer at its root and shoot tips?
check.why: Apical meristems are regions of dividing cells at the tips of roots and shoots.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Growth is an irreversible increase in size or mass; development is specialisation. Use dry mass to avoid water effects, and remember the sigmoid curve's lag, exponential and stationary phases when comparing treatments.

content.problem: Two bean plants are measured daily. Plant A gains fresh mass quickly but its dry mass hardly changes; plant B gains dry mass steadily. Which is really growing and why?

steps.reason: Fresh mass includes water, which can rise without new tissue.
steps.result: Plant A may only be taking up water.
steps.predictPrompt: What does dry mass show?

steps.reason: Dry mass measures new cell material after water is removed.
steps.result: Plant B is adding real tissue.

steps.reason: Growth also involves cell division and development.
steps.result: Plant B is growing; Plant A needs more evidence such as height or cell counts.

content.question: Why can a plant keep growing taller for many years while a mouse stops growing at adult size?
hints: Plants keep meristems at their tips and in their stems.
Animals grow throughout the body and reach a fixed adult size.
Meristems continue to divide throughout the plant's life.

lessons.title: Seed Germination
lessons.objective: Explain the conditions needed for germination and describe the sequence from water uptake to seedling establishment.

content.heading: Seed germination
paragraphs: A dry maize seed can sit in a jar for months, then sprout within days when it is planted and watered. Something switches the dormant embryo back to life.

content.heading: Conditions needed for germination
paragraphs: A seed needs a viable embryo, water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Water is absorbed first, softening the seed coat and activating enzymes; oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration, and warmth speeds up the enzyme-controlled reactions.

Light is not needed by every seed, but some seeds germinate only in light or only in darkness. The seed also needs enough stored food, and the seedling needs light and minerals once it starts photosynthesising.
A seed that fails to germinate may be dead, dormant, too dry, waterlogged or attacked by fungi. Testing a sample for viability and using clean, well-drained soil improves establishment.
bullets: Viable embryo, water, oxygen and suitable temperature.
Water activates enzymes; oxygen powers respiration.
Light requirements vary; dead or dormant seeds will not sprout.
content.takeaway: Water wakes the seed; oxygen and warmth drive the engine.

check.question: Why does a waterlogged seed often fail to germinate?
check.why: Water fills the air spaces in the soil, so the seed cannot obtain enough oxygen for aerobic respiration.

content.heading: The sequence of germination
paragraphs: Germination begins with imbibition, the uptake of water through the seed coat. The seed swells, enzymes are activated, and stored starch, protein and oil are broken down into soluble substances that can be transported to the embryo.

The radicle emerges first and grows downwards, anchoring the seedling and absorbing water. The plumule then emerges and grows upwards, and the stem elongates; in many seeds a hook forms to protect the delicate shoot tip as it pushes through the soil.

The seedling relies on stored food until its first leaves expand and photosynthesis begins. At that point, the food store shrinks, the seedling becomes independent, and growth switches to light-driven sugar production.
bullets: Imbibition activates enzymes that digest stored food.
Radicle emerges first; plumule follows.
Photosynthesis begins when the first leaves expand.
content.takeaway: The seed digests its store, sends down a root, then sends up a shoot.

check.question: Which part normally emerges first during germination?
check.why: The radicle emerges first, anchors the seedling and begins water uptake.

content.heading: Dormancy and delayed germination
paragraphs: Dormancy is a state in which a viable seed does not germinate even when conditions seem suitable. A hard seed coat, an immature embryo or chemical inhibitors inside the seed can delay germination until the environment improves.

Farmers and gardeners break dormancy by scarifying the seed coat, soaking or chilling the seed, or removing the fleshy fruit around it. These treatments imitate the natural weathering, fire or passage through an animal's gut that would break the coat.

Dormancy is useful in the wild because it spreads germination over time and avoids a whole generation sprouting in a short wet spell. In agriculture, uniform germination is preferred, so seed treatments are used to synchronise emergence.
bullets: Dormancy: a viable seed fails to germinate despite suitable conditions.
Hard coats, immature embryos and inhibitors cause dormancy.
Scarification, soaking and chilling break dormancy.
content.takeaway: Dormancy is a safety switch that waits for the right moment.

check.question: A hard seed coat delays germination because it
check.why: The coat blocks water and oxygen, so imbibition and respiration cannot begin.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Germination needs a viable seed, water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Imbibition activates enzymes, the radicle emerges first, and the plumule follows. Dormancy delays germination until conditions improve, and the seedling becomes independent when its leaves expand.

content.problem: A farmer plants maize seeds in cold, waterlogged soil and few seedlings appear. Explain two likely causes and one remedy.

steps.reason: Waterlogged soil has little air, so the seed cannot respire aerobically.
steps.result: Germination is slow or fails.
steps.predictPrompt: What about the temperature?

steps.reason: Cold soil slows enzyme activity and imbibition.
steps.result: Seeds remain dormant or germinate unevenly.

steps.reason: Plant when the soil is warm and well drained.
steps.result: Better aeration and temperature improve germination.

content.question: Why does a seed need oxygen before its first leaf appears?
hints: The embryo is already respiring.
Aerobic respiration releases ATP from stored food.
Without oxygen, germination stalls even if water is present.

lessons.title: Epigeal and Hypogeal Germination
lessons.objective: Differentiate epigeal from hypogeal germination, give examples of each, and relate the pattern to seedling survival.

content.heading: Epigeal and hypogeal germination
paragraphs: A bean seedling lifts its two thick seed leaves above the soil, while a maize seedling sends up a rolled shoot and keeps its seed leaves underground. The difference is called epigeal versus hypogeal germination.

content.heading: Epigeal germination
paragraphs: In epigeal germination, the hypocotyl, the region below the cotyledons, elongates and pushes the cotyledons above the soil. The cotyledons turn green and photosynthesise for a time before they shrivel and drop.
The hypocotyl often forms a hook as it emerges, protecting the delicate plumule from damage as it pushes through the soil. Bean, castor and sunflower are standard examples.

Because the cotyledons leave the seed and enter the light, the seedling can start photosynthesis early. The cost is that the exposed cotyledons and shoot are vulnerable to frost, grazing and drying. This early start can give the seedling an advantage in a sunny gap.
bullets: Hypocotyl elongates and lifts the cotyledons above ground.
Cotyledons turn green and photosynthesise before shrinking.
Examples: bean, castor and sunflower.
content.takeaway: Epigeal germination lifts its seed leaves into the light.

check.question: In epigeal germination, the cotyledons are carried above the soil by the
check.why: The hypocotyl is the region below the cotyledons, and its elongation lifts them above the soil.

content.heading: Hypogeal germination
paragraphs: In hypogeal germination, the cotyledons remain below the soil and the epicotyl, the region above the cotyledons, elongates to push up the plumule. The cotyledons stay in the seed and supply food rather than turning green.

Maize, pea, rice and groundnut are standard examples. The shoot emerges as a tight spike or rolled leaf, which reduces friction and protects the growing tip. The protected shoot can push through a crusted soil surface.
Keeping the cotyledons underground protects the food store and the shoot base from frost, grazing and drying. The seedling depends on stored food for longer, so it may grow more slowly at first.
bullets: Epicotyl elongates and pushes the plumule above ground.
Cotyledons stay below ground and supply food.
Examples: maize, pea, rice and groundnut.
content.takeaway: Hypogeal germination keeps its food store underground.

check.question: Which plant shows hypogeal germination?
check.why: Maize cotyledons remain below ground while the epicotyl pushes the plumule upwards.

content.heading: Comparing the two patterns
paragraphs: The key difference is the position of the cotyledons and the region that elongates. Epigeal seedlings lift their cotyledons with the hypocotyl; hypogeal seedlings keep them below ground while the epicotyl elongates.

The pattern affects planting depth and early survival. Epigeal seeds should not be buried too deeply, because the hypocotyl must reach the surface; hypogeal seeds can be planted deeper, since the food store stays protected.

Neither pattern is universally better. Epigeal seedlings gain early photosynthesis but are exposed; hypogeal seedlings are protected but rely on stored food for longer, which matters in poor light or cold soil.
bullets: Epigeal: cotyledons above ground, hypocotyl elongates.
Hypogeal: cotyledons below ground, epicotyl elongates.
Planting depth and exposure differ between the two.
content.takeaway: Cotyledon position and the elongating region separate the two patterns.

check.question: The main difference between epigeal and hypogeal germination is the
options: Number of seeds in the fruit
check.why: Epigeal cotyledons rise above the soil, while hypogeal cotyledons remain below it.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Epigeal: hypocotyl lifts cotyledons above ground, as in bean and castor. Hypogeal: epicotyl lifts the plumule while cotyledons stay below ground, as in maize and pea. Plant epigeal seeds shallower than hypogeal seeds.

content.problem: A gardener plants bean and maize seeds at the same depth. The maize emerges well, but many bean seedlings fail. Explain the difference.

steps.reason: Bean is epigeal and maize is hypogeal.
steps.result: Bean lifts its cotyledons; maize keeps them below ground.
steps.predictPrompt: Why would depth affect the bean more?

steps.reason: The bean hypocotyl must push the cotyledons to the surface.
steps.result: Deep planting exhausts the seedling before it reaches light.

steps.reason: The maize food store stays underground and the epicotyl is adapted to push through.
steps.result: Maize emerges from the same depth more successfully.

content.question: Why might a farmer plant bean seeds more shallowly than maize seeds?
hints: Bean is epigeal and must lift its cotyledons to the surface.
Maize is hypogeal and its food store stays underground.
Deep planting uses up the bean's stored food before the shoot reaches light.

lessons.title: Nervous Coordination and Neurons
lessons.objective: Explain the need for coordination, compare nervous and hormonal control, and describe neuron structure, impulse transmission and synapses.

content.heading: Nervous coordination and neurons
paragraphs: A student touches a hot plate and pulls the hand away before thinking about it. Receptors, neurons and muscles have already coordinated the response.

content.heading: Why coordination matters
paragraphs: Coordination links a stimulus to a response. A receptor detects the stimulus, a coordinator processes the information, and an effector such as a muscle or gland carries out the response; this sequence keeps the body working as a whole.

The nervous system provides fast, short-lived control through electrical impulses and chemical synapses. The endocrine system provides slower, longer-lasting control through hormones carried in the blood.

Both systems maintain homeostasis. Nervous control suits rapid actions such as blinking or balancing, while hormonal control suits gradual changes such as growth, puberty and blood glucose regulation.
bullets: Stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response.
Nervous control is fast and short-lived; hormonal control is slower and longer-lasting.
Both systems help maintain a steady internal environment.
content.takeaway: Nerves switch responses quickly; hormones tune the body slowly.

check.question: Which sequence correctly describes a coordinated response?
check.why: A stimulus is detected by a receptor, processed by a coordinator and answered by an effector.

content.heading: The neuron
paragraphs: A neuron is a nerve cell specialised for carrying impulses. It has a cell body containing the nucleus, dendrites that receive signals, and a long axon that carries the impulse away towards another cell.

Many axons are wrapped in a fatty myelin sheath, which insulates the fibre and speeds up transmission. The sheath is interrupted at nodes of Ranvier, where the impulse jumps from node to node in saltatory conduction.

Sensory neurons carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system, motor neurons carry impulses from the central nervous system to effectors, and relay neurons connect the two inside the brain or spinal cord.
bullets: Dendrites receive; the axon transmits; the cell body contains the nucleus.
Myelin insulates and speeds up the impulse.
Sensory, motor and relay neurons have different jobs.
content.takeaway: A neuron is built to receive, carry and pass on an impulse.

check.question: Which part of a neuron carries impulses away from the cell body?
check.why: The axon is the long fibre that conducts the impulse away from the cell body.

content.heading: Impulse transmission and synapses
paragraphs: At rest, the neuron membrane is polarised, with a negative charge inside and a positive charge outside. A stimulus makes the membrane permeable to sodium ions, which rush in and reverse the charge; this is the action potential.

The impulse travels along the axon as a wave of depolarisation. Behind it, potassium ions move out and restore the resting charge, so the neuron can carry another impulse after a short recovery period.

At a synapse, the impulse cannot jump the gap. The presynaptic knob releases a neurotransmitter such as acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft; the chemical binds to receptors on the next neuron and starts a new impulse, so transmission is one-way.
bullets: Action potential: sodium ions enter and reverse the membrane charge.
Potassium ions restore the resting potential.
Neurotransmitters carry the signal across the synaptic cleft in one direction.
content.takeaway: Electric along the axon, chemical across the synapse.

check.question: The gap between two neurons is crossed by
check.why: Neurotransmitters diffuse across the synaptic cleft and bind to receptors on the next neuron.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Nervous control is fast and short-lived; hormonal control is slower and longer-lasting. Neurons carry impulses, myelin speeds them up, and neurotransmitters cross synapses in one direction, so signals travel one way only.

content.problem: A toxin blocks acetylcholine receptors at a synapse. Predict the effect on a muscle and explain why.

steps.reason: Acetylcholine normally binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
steps.result: The signal cannot pass from the motor neuron to the muscle.
steps.predictPrompt: What happens to the muscle?

steps.reason: Without a new impulse, the muscle fibre is not stimulated.
steps.result: The muscle cannot contract and becomes weak or paralysed.

steps.reason: Synapses transmit in one direction only.
steps.result: The block stops communication at that synapse, not along the axon behind it.

content.question: Why does a reflex withdrawal from a hot object happen before the person feels the pain?
hints: The reflex arc can complete in the spinal cord.
The brain receives the sensory information at the same time.
Feeling and conscious interpretation take longer than the spinal response.

lessons.title: Brain, Spinal Cord and Reflexes
lessons.objective: Describe the central nervous system, the main regions of the brain, the spinal cord, and how reflex arcs produce fast involuntary responses.

content.heading: Brain, spinal cord and reflexes
paragraphs: A footballer ducks a flying ball, and a student blinks as dust blows into the eye. Both responses depend on the central nervous system, which sorts the signal and triggers the action.

content.heading: The central nervous system
paragraphs: A footballer ducks a ball and a student blinks as dust blows into the eye. Both responses run through the central nervous system, which sorts signals and issues commands.

The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord. The brain sits in the skull, the spinal cord runs inside the vertebral column, and both are wrapped in membranes called meninges and cushioned by cerebrospinal fluid.

Inside, grey matter holds cell bodies and synapses, while white matter holds myelinated axons. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is the network of cranial and spinal nerves linking the CNS to receptors and effectors.
bullets: CNS: brain and spinal cord; PNS: cranial and spinal nerves.
Meninges and cerebrospinal fluid protect the CNS.
Grey matter holds cell bodies; white matter is myelinated.
content.takeaway: The CNS is the control centre; the PNS is the wiring.

check.question: Which structure cushions the brain and spinal cord in fluid?
check.why: Cerebrospinal fluid surrounds and cushions the CNS, while the meninges are the membranes that enclose it.

content.heading: The brain and spinal cord
paragraphs: Different regions of the brain do different jobs. The cerebrum, with its folded outer layer, handles conscious thought, memory, language, vision, hearing and voluntary movement. The cerebellum, behind it, coordinates balance, posture and smooth muscle action.

The medulla oblongata at the base of the brain controls involuntary activities such as breathing, heart rate and blood pressure. The hypothalamus monitors temperature, hunger and thirst, and links the nervous system to the pituitary gland.
The spinal cord is more than a cable. It carries sensory impulses up and motor impulses down, and it contains reflex centres that produce fast responses without waiting for the brain.
bullets: Cerebrum: thought, memory, senses and voluntary movement.
Cerebellum: balance, posture and smooth muscle control.
Medulla and hypothalamus: involuntary control and internal balance.
content.takeaway: The brain decides; the spinal cord can also act alone.

check.question: Which part of the brain controls balance and coordination?
check.why: The cerebellum coordinates balance, posture and smooth muscle action.

content.heading: Reflex and voluntary actions
paragraphs: A reflex action is a rapid, automatic and involuntary response to a stimulus. It protects the body before the brain has time to think.

The pathway is called a reflex arc. It runs from receptor to sensory neuron, then to a relay neuron in the spinal cord, then to a motor neuron and an effector such as a muscle. Blinking, the knee jerk and pulling the hand from a hot object are simple reflexes.

A voluntary action begins in the brain and is under conscious control, so it is slower and can be learned or stopped. A conditioned reflex is a learned link between a stimulus and a response, such as salivating at the smell of food or automatically braking a bicycle.
bullets: Reflex arc: receptor → sensory neuron → relay → motor neuron → effector.
Reflexes are rapid, involuntary and protective.
Voluntary actions are conscious; conditioned reflexes are learned.
content.takeaway: Reflexes take the short road; voluntary actions take the long one.

check.question: Which sequence correctly shows a reflex arc?
options: Receptor → motor neuron → relay neuron → sensory neuron → effector
Receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron → motor neuron → effector
Effector → sensory neuron → relay neuron → motor neuron → receptor
Receptor → relay neuron → sensory neuron → effector → motor neuron
check.why: A reflex arc runs from receptor to sensory neuron, relay neuron, motor neuron and effector.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord, protected by meninges and cerebrospinal fluid. The cerebrum handles conscious activity, the cerebellum balance, and the medulla involuntary functions. Reflex arcs pass through the spinal cord for speed.

content.problem: A doctor taps a patient's knee and the leg kicks out, but the patient feels nothing until afterwards. Explain the pathway and why the response is involuntary.

steps.reason: The tap stretches a tendon, and stretch receptors in the thigh muscle detect the change.
steps.result: A sensory impulse starts towards the spinal cord.
steps.predictPrompt: Where does the impulse go next?

steps.reason: The sensory neuron synapses with a relay neuron in the spinal cord, which synapses with a motor neuron.
steps.result: The motor neuron stimulates the thigh muscle to contract.

steps.reason: The response leaves the spinal cord before the brain has processed the signal.
steps.result: The leg kicks automatically, and the brain is informed afterwards.

content.question: Why does a person blink when an object comes towards the eye, even when they try to keep the eye open?
hints: Blinking is a protective reflex.
The reflex arc can be completed quickly through the brain stem.
Conscious control is slower than the reflex pathway.

lessons.title: Skin, Nose and Tongue
lessons.objective: Relate the structure and function of the skin, nose and tongue to touch, smell and taste, and explain common defects of these sense organs.

content.heading: Skin, nose and tongue
paragraphs: A hand feels the roughness of bark, the nose catches smoke, and the tongue detects salt in soup. Each sense organ turns a different kind of stimulus into nerve impulses.

content.heading: The skin as a tactile organ
paragraphs: The skin is the largest sense organ. Its dermis contains several kinds of receptor: touch corpuscles near the surface, deeper pressure corpuscles, separate cold and heat receptors, and free nerve endings for pain.
The receptors are unevenly distributed. Fingertips, lips and the tongue carry many touch receptors, which is why they detect fine detail, while the back is much less sensitive.

Receptors also adapt. A ring left on the finger soon feels normal because the touch receptors stop responding to a constant stimulus, yet a new change is detected at once. This is why we notice a fly landing but not the feel of clothing.
bullets: Skin receptors detect touch, pressure, temperature and pain.
Fingertips and lips are most sensitive because they have more receptors.
Receptors adapt to a constant stimulus.
content.takeaway: Skin reports touch, pressure, temperature and pain.

check.question: A ring feels tight when first worn but soon becomes unnoticeable. This is due to
check.why: Receptors stop responding to an unchanging stimulus, so the ring is no longer noticed.

content.heading: The nose and smell
paragraphs: The nose detects chemicals in the air. At the roof of the nasal cavity, the olfactory epithelium contains receptor cells with fine cilia, and mucus dissolves arriving molecules so they can bind to the receptors.

The receptor cells send impulses along the olfactory nerve to the cerebrum, where the smell is identified. A blocked nose, a cold or damaged receptor cells can cause anosmia, the loss of the sense of smell.
Smell and taste work together. Much of what we call flavour comes from odours rising from the mouth into the nasal cavity, so food tastes bland when the nose is blocked.
bullets: Olfactory receptor cells sit in the roof of the nasal cavity.
Mucus dissolves odour molecules so receptors can detect them.
Blocked noses cause anosmia and dull the taste of food.
content.takeaway: The nose reads dissolved chemicals and sends smell signals to the brain.

check.question: Why does food taste bland when you have a cold?
options: Odour molecules cannot reach the olfactory receptors
check.why: A blocked nose prevents odour molecules from reaching the olfactory receptors, so the smell component of flavour is lost.

content.heading: The tongue and taste
paragraphs: The tongue detects dissolved chemicals through taste buds, which sit in small bumps called papillae. Each bud contains receptor cells that respond to one or more of five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.

Impulses travel along cranial nerves to the medulla and then to the cerebrum. Taste is not fixed to a single zone: the old tongue map is wrong, because most of the tongue can detect every taste, though sensitivity varies.

Taste buds are damaged by very hot food, and their sensitivity falls when the mouth is dry because chemicals cannot dissolve. Smoking and some medicines also dull taste, while ageing reduces the number of working buds.
bullets: Taste buds detect sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.
Taste impulses travel by cranial nerves to the brain.
Heat, dryness and ageing damage or dull taste buds.
content.takeaway: The tongue identifies dissolved chemicals as five basic tastes.

check.question: Which list gives the five basic tastes?
check.why: The five basic tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Skin receptors detect touch, pressure, temperature and pain and adapt to constant stimuli. The nose detects dissolved odours, and the tongue detects five basic tastes. Smell and taste combine to produce flavour.

content.problem: A cook loses the sense of smell after a head injury and complains that food has lost its flavour, although tests show normal taste buds. Explain the observation.

steps.reason: The tongue and taste buds still detect the five basic tastes.
steps.result: The cook can still tell sweet from sour or salty.
steps.predictPrompt: Why is flavour still missing?

steps.reason: The injury has damaged the olfactory pathway, so odours cannot reach the brain.
steps.result: The smell component of flavour is lost.

steps.reason: The brain builds flavour from both taste and smell.
steps.result: Food tastes bland even though the tongue is working.

content.question: Why can a person still recognise sweet and salty foods when the nose is blocked, but not the full flavour of a meal?
hints: Taste buds detect basic tastes without help from the nose.
Most flavour comes from odours reaching the olfactory epithelium.
The brain combines taste and smell into one experience.

lessons.title: The Eye
lessons.objective: Describe the structure of the eye, explain focusing and the pupil reflex, and identify common eye defects and their corrections.

content.heading: The eye
paragraphs: The eye turns light into nerve impulses. Its curved surfaces focus light on a light-sensitive retina, and the brain builds the image we see.

content.heading: Structure of the eye
paragraphs: Light enters the eye through the transparent cornea and passes through the pupil, the hole controlled by the coloured iris. The lens then focuses the light onto the retina at the back of the eye.

The retina contains rods, which work in dim light but see only black and white, and cones, which detect colour and sharp detail in bright light. The fovea has the highest concentration of cones and gives the clearest vision.

The optic nerve carries impulses from the retina to the brain. Where it leaves the eye there are no receptor cells, creating a blind spot. The sclera is the tough white outer coat, and the choroid supplies blood.
bullets: Cornea and lens focus light; iris controls pupil size.
Rods work in dim light; cones detect colour and detail.
Optic nerve carries impulses; the blind spot has no receptors.
content.takeaway: The eye focuses light and the retina converts it to impulses.

check.question: Which cells in the retina are responsible for colour vision?
check.why: Cones detect colour and sharp detail in bright light.

content.heading: Focusing and the pupil reflex
paragraphs: The eye focuses by changing the shape of the lens, a process called accommodation. To look at something close, the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments slacken, and the lens becomes thicker; to look far away, the muscles relax and the lens becomes thinner.

The pupil reflex controls how much light enters. In bright light the circular muscles of the iris contract and the radial muscles relax, so the pupil narrows. In dim light the reverse happens and the pupil widens.

These responses are reflexes, not conscious decisions. The retina detects the light level and the brain stem sends the command, protecting the retina from bright light and letting in more light when it is dark.
bullets: Accommodation: ciliary muscles change lens thickness.
Bright light constricts the pupil; dim light dilates it.
Both are reflexes controlled by the nervous system.
content.takeaway: Near vision thickens the lens; bright light narrows the pupil.

check.question: To focus on a nearby object, the ciliary muscles
options: Relax and the lens becomes thinner
Contract and the lens becomes thicker
check.why: Near vision requires the ciliary muscles to contract, slackening the suspensory ligaments so the lens becomes thicker.

content.heading: Defects of the eye
paragraphs: Short sight, or myopia, happens when the eyeball is too long or the lens too strong, so distant images focus in front of the retina. It is corrected with a concave lens that spreads the rays before they enter the eye.

Long sight, or hypermetropia, happens when the eyeball is too short or the lens too weak, so near images focus behind the retina. A convex lens brings the rays together. Astigmatism is caused by an uneven cornea or lens and is corrected with a cylindrical lens.

Other defects include presbyopia, the loss of lens elasticity with age; cataract, a clouding of the lens; glaucoma, raised pressure inside the eye; and colour blindness, usually a defect in the red or green cones.
bullets: Myopia: distant blur, concave lens.
Hypermetropia: near blur, convex lens.
Cataract, glaucoma and colour blindness also affect sight.
content.takeaway: Match the defect to its lens: concave for short sight, convex for long sight.

check.question: A person cannot see distant objects clearly. Which defect and correction are correct?
check.why: Myopia is short sight, and a concave lens spreads the rays so the image falls on the retina.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: The cornea and lens focus light on the retina, where rods and cones make impulses. Near vision thickens the lens; bright light constricts the pupil. Myopia needs a concave lens and hypermetropia a convex lens.

content.problem: A student complains that the board is blurry but reading a book is fine. Identify the likely defect, explain where the image falls, and state the correction.

steps.reason: Clear near vision with blurred distant vision is short sight.
steps.result: The student probably has myopia.
steps.predictPrompt: Where does the image form?

steps.reason: In myopia the eyeball is too long or the lens too strong.
steps.result: Distant rays focus in front of the retina.

steps.reason: A concave lens spreads the rays before they enter the eye.
steps.result: The image moves back onto the retina.

content.question: Why does the pupil become smaller in bright sunlight even when a person tries to keep it open?
hints: The pupil reflex is involuntary.
The retina detects the light level.
Circular muscles of the iris contract in bright light.

lessons.title: The Ear
lessons.objective: Describe the structure of the ear, explain how sound is converted into impulses, describe balance, and identify common ear defects.

content.heading: The ear
paragraphs: The ear turns sound waves into nerve impulses. It also contains organs of balance, which tell the brain how the head is moving.

content.heading: Structure and hearing
paragraphs: Sound waves are collected by the pinna and travel down the auditory canal to the tympanum, or eardrum. The eardrum vibrates and passes the vibration through three small bones, the malleus, incus and stapes, to the oval window.
From the oval window, the vibrations enter the fluid-filled cochlea. Hair cells inside the cochlea convert the vibrations into nerve impulses, which travel along the auditory nerve to the brain.

The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the back of the throat and keeps air pressure equal on both sides of the eardrum. The ossicles also amplify the vibration, because the middle ear must transfer energy from air to fluid.
bullets: Pinna and canal collect sound; eardrum vibrates.
Ossicles pass vibrations to the cochlea.
Hair cells make impulses; the auditory nerve carries them.
content.takeaway: Sound travels as vibrations until hair cells make impulses.

check.question: Which structure converts sound vibrations into nerve impulses?
check.why: Hair cells in the cochlea convert vibrations into impulses carried by the auditory nerve.

content.heading: Balance and the inner ear
paragraphs: Balance is detected by the vestibular system in the inner ear. Three semicircular canals, set at right angles to each other, contain fluid that moves when the head rotates, bending hair cells and signalling the direction of movement.
The utricle and saccule detect straight-line acceleration and the pull of gravity. They contain small stones called otoliths that press on hair cells when the head tilts or moves.

Impulses from these organs travel to the cerebellum and other brain centres, which adjust posture and eye movements. Spinning quickly disturbs the fluid, so the brain still receives movement signals after stopping, which causes dizziness.
bullets: Semicircular canals detect rotation of the head.
Utricle and saccule detect gravity and straight-line movement.
Balance signals go to the cerebellum.
content.takeaway: Canals sense turning; otolith organs sense gravity and speed.

check.question: Which part of the ear detects rotational movement of the head?
check.why: Fluid in the semicircular canals moves when the head rotates, bending hair cells.

content.heading: Defects of the ear
paragraphs: Conductive deafness happens when sound cannot reach the inner ear. Causes include wax blocking the canal, a torn eardrum, fluid from otitis media, or damaged ossicles; hearing aids often help because they make the sound louder.

Sensorineural deafness happens when hair cells or the auditory nerve are damaged, for example by very loud noise, some medicines, infection or ageing. It is usually permanent, and a cochlear implant may restore some hearing by stimulating the nerve directly.
