Tinnitus is a ringing in the ears without an external sound, while Ménière's disease causes episodes of dizziness, hearing loss and a blocked feeling. Ear infections are common in children because their Eustachian tubes are short and horizontal.
bullets: Conductive deafness: sound blocked; hearing aids help.
Sensorineural deafness: hair cells or nerve damaged; often permanent.
Otitis media and loud noise are common causes.
content.takeaway: Blocked sound is conductive; damaged nerve is sensorineural.

check.question: Damage to the hair cells of the cochlea causes which type of deafness?
check.why: Hair cell damage affects the conversion of vibrations into impulses, which is sensorineural deafness.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Sound passes from pinna to eardrum, ossicles, cochlea and auditory nerve. Semicircular canals detect rotation, while the utricle and saccule detect gravity. Conductive deafness blocks sound; sensorineural deafness damages hair cells or the nerve.

content.problem: A factory worker develops hearing loss after years of loud noise, while another person loses hearing because wax blocks the ear canal. Distinguish the two types and their likely outcomes.

steps.reason: Loud noise damages hair cells in the cochlea.
steps.result: The worker has sensorineural deafness.
steps.predictPrompt: Is it likely to recover?

steps.reason: Wax prevents sound from reaching the eardrum and inner ear.
steps.result: The second person has conductive deafness.

steps.reason: Wax can be removed, but damaged hair cells do not usually regenerate.
steps.result: Conductive loss is often reversible; sensorineural loss is usually permanent.

content.question: Why does a cold often cause temporary hearing loss and a blocked feeling in the ear?
hints: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the throat.
A cold causes swelling and mucus in that tube.
Unequal pressure on the eardrum reduces its movement.

lessons.title: Animal Hormones
lessons.objective: State the location of the main endocrine glands, relate each hormone to its function, and explain disorders caused by hormone imbalance.

content.heading: Animal hormones
paragraphs: Hormones are chemical messengers carried in the blood. They act on target organs more slowly than nerves, but their effects usually last longer.

content.heading: The endocrine system and the pituitary
paragraphs: An endocrine gland has no duct. It releases hormones straight into the blood, and the hormone acts only on cells that carry the matching receptor, called target cells.

The pituitary gland sits at the base of the brain, attached to the hypothalamus. It is called the master gland because it controls several other glands. Its anterior lobe releases growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, adrenocorticotrophic hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinising hormone; the posterior lobe releases antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin.
Growth hormone promotes growth of bones and muscles. Too little in childhood causes dwarfism, too much causes gigantism, and excess in adulthood causes acromegaly.
bullets: Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into blood.
The pituitary is attached to the hypothalamus and controls other glands.
Growth hormone excess or deficiency changes body growth.
content.takeaway: The pituitary is the master gland because it commands other glands.

check.question: Which gland is called the master gland because it controls other endocrine glands?
check.why: The pituitary releases hormones that control the thyroid, adrenal cortex and gonads.

content.heading: Thyroid, parathyroid and adrenal glands
paragraphs: The thyroid gland lies in the neck, just below the larynx. It releases thyroxine, which controls the rate of metabolism and needs iodine to be made. A lack of iodine causes goitre, an enlarged thyroid, while too little thyroxine in a child causes cretinism and in an adult causes myxoedema.

The parathyroid glands, embedded in the thyroid, release parathormone, which raises blood calcium. The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys. The cortex releases cortisol, which helps the body cope with stress, and aldosterone, which controls salt balance.
The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and noradrenaline. In danger, adrenaline raises heart rate, widens the airways and releases glucose, preparing the body for fight or flight.
bullets: Thyroxine controls metabolism and needs iodine.
Parathormone raises blood calcium.
Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight.
content.takeaway: Thyroid sets the metabolic rate; adrenaline meets emergencies.

check.question: Which hormone raises blood calcium?
check.why: Parathormone from the parathyroid glands raises the level of calcium in the blood.

content.heading: Pancreas and gonads
paragraphs: The pancreas contains small groups of cells called the islets of Langerhans. Beta cells release insulin, which lowers blood glucose by helping cells take up glucose and the liver store it as glycogen; alpha cells release glucagon, which raises blood glucose by converting glycogen back to glucose.

Too little insulin causes diabetes mellitus, with high blood glucose, thirst, frequent urination and glucose in the urine. The ovaries release oestrogen and progesterone, which control the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and female secondary sexual characteristics.

The testes release testosterone, which controls sperm production and male secondary sexual characteristics. These hormones are carried in the blood but act only on target organs that have the matching receptors.
bullets: Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it.
Ovaries release oestrogen and progesterone.
Testes release testosterone.
content.takeaway: Insulin and glucagon are opposites; the gonads set sexual development.

check.question: Which cells release insulin?
check.why: Beta cells in the islets of Langerhans release insulin, which lowers blood glucose.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Pituitary: growth and control of other glands. Thyroid: thyroxine and metabolism. Parathyroid: calcium. Adrenal: cortisol, aldosterone and adrenaline. Pancreas: insulin and glucagon. Gonads: sex hormones. Learn each gland with its hormone and one disorder.

content.problem: A patient is always thirsty, passes urine often and has glucose in the blood. Which gland and hormone are involved, and what is the probable condition?

steps.reason: Thirst, frequent urination and glucose in the urine point to high blood glucose.
steps.result: The patient may have diabetes mellitus.
steps.predictPrompt: Which hormone normally lowers glucose?

steps.reason: Insulin from the beta cells of the pancreas lowers blood glucose.
steps.result: Too little insulin explains the high glucose.

steps.reason: Glucose in the filtrate draws water into the urine by osmosis.
steps.result: The patient passes large volumes of urine and becomes thirsty.

content.question: Why does adrenaline make the heart beat faster and the breathing rate rise during an emergency?
hints: Adrenaline is released from the adrenal medulla.
Muscles need more oxygen and glucose for action.
The response prepares the body for fight or flight.

lessons.title: Plant Hormones
lessons.objective: Describe the functions of auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene, and relate phytohormones to plant responses and agricultural use.

content.heading: Plant hormones
paragraphs: Plants have no nerves, yet they still respond to light, gravity and touch. Chemical messengers called phytohormones coordinate their growth and development, and their effects depend on concentration and tissue.

content.heading: Auxins and tropisms
paragraphs: Auxins are made in the shoot tips, root tips and young leaves. They move from cell to cell and can spread sideways, so the side of a shoot that receives less light collects more auxin.

In a shoot, high auxin concentration makes cells elongate. The shaded side therefore grows faster than the lit side, and the shoot bends towards the light, which is positive phototropism. In a root, the same high concentration inhibits elongation, so the lower side grows more slowly and the root bends downwards, which is positive geotropism.
Auxin also causes apical dominance: the growing tip produces auxin that suppresses the growth of side buds. Removing the tip releases those buds and makes the plant bushier.
bullets: Auxin is made at shoot and root tips.
Uneven auxin makes shoots bend towards light and roots downwards.
Apical dominance suppresses side buds.
content.takeaway: Auxin redistributes growth; the darker side grows more.

check.question: A shoot bends towards light because auxin
options: Collects on the dark side and makes cells elongate
Collects on the light side and makes cells elongate
Is destroyed by light on both sides
check.why: Auxin gathers on the shaded side, where it makes cells elongate so that side grows faster and the shoot bends towards the light.

content.heading: Gibberellins and cytokinins
paragraphs: Gibberellins are growth promoters that stimulate stem elongation, seed germination and fruit development. During germination, gibberellin moves from the embryo to the aleurone layer of the seed and triggers the production of amylase, which digests stored starch into maltose for the growing seedling.

Cytokinins stimulate cell division and delay the ageing of leaves. They are produced mainly in root tips and move upwards in the xylem, and they also promote the growth of side shoots and the mobilisation of nutrients towards young tissues.
Growers use these hormones in agriculture. Gibberellin can make seedless grapes larger and break dormancy in some seeds, while cytokinins are used to keep cut leaves and flowers fresh for longer.
bullets: Gibberellins promote stem growth, germination and fruit development.
Cytokinins promote cell division and delay ageing.
Both are used in agriculture and horticulture.
content.takeaway: Gibberellins stretch and wake seeds; cytokinins divide and delay decay.

check.question: Which hormone breaks seed dormancy by triggering amylase production?
check.why: Gibberellin stimulates the aleurone layer to produce amylase, which digests stored starch for the embryo.

content.heading: Abscisic acid and ethylene
paragraphs: Abscisic acid is the main growth inhibitor. It builds up when a plant is short of water, closes the stomata to reduce water loss, and keeps seeds dormant until conditions improve. It also slows growth and helps leaves and fruits fall.

Ethylene is a gas that acts as a hormone. It speeds up the ripening of fruit, the ageing of flowers and the abscission of leaves and fruits. Because it is a gas, ethylene from one ripening fruit can trigger ripening in its neighbours.
Farmers and traders use these effects. Ethylene is used to ripen bananas and tomatoes uniformly, while chemicals that block ethylene slow ripening and reduce spoilage during storage and transport.
bullets: Abscisic acid closes stomata and maintains dormancy.
Ethylene ripens fruit and promotes abscission.
Both are used to control ripening and storage.
content.takeaway: ABA puts the brakes on; ethylene moves ripening along.

check.question: Which gas promotes the ripening of fruit?
check.why: Ethylene is a gaseous hormone that speeds up fruit ripening and the ageing of plant parts.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Auxin drives phototropism and apical dominance. Gibberellins promote stem growth and germination. Cytokinins promote cell division. Abscisic acid closes stomata and keeps seeds dormant, while ethylene ripens fruit and causes abscission.

content.problem: A farmer picks tomatoes while they are still green so they can survive transport. Explain how ethylene can be used, and why the storage room must be ventilated.

steps.reason: Ethylene speeds up the changes that soften and colour fruit.
steps.result: The green tomatoes ripen uniformly before sale.
steps.predictPrompt: Why ventilate the room?

steps.reason: Ethylene is a gas, so it spreads from fruit to fruit.
steps.result: One ripening fruit can trigger ripening in the whole batch.

steps.reason: Ventilation removes excess ethylene and slows over-ripening.
steps.result: Spoilage is reduced and the fruit lasts longer.

content.question: Why does removing the shoot tip of a hedge make it grow bushier?
hints: The shoot tip is the main source of auxin.
Auxin suppresses the growth of side buds.
Removing the tip releases the side buds from apical dominance.

lessons.title: Homeostasis
lessons.objective: Explain homeostasis and negative feedback, describe temperature regulation, and explain how the kidneys control salt and water balance.

content.heading: Homeostasis
paragraphs: Your body keeps its temperature, water and salt within narrow limits even when the weather changes. This steady internal state is called homeostasis, and nerves and hormones do the adjusting.

content.heading: The principle of homeostasis
paragraphs: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a steady internal environment despite changes outside the body. It keeps temperature, blood glucose, water and salt within narrow limits so that enzymes and cells can work properly.

Control usually works by negative feedback. A receptor detects a change, a coordinator such as the hypothalamus compares it with the set point, and an effector produces a response that reverses the change. When temperature rises, for example, the body cools itself and the rise is corrected.

Negative feedback keeps conditions stable rather than perfectly constant. Values drift above and below the set point, and the response always pushes them back towards it. Positive feedback, which amplifies a change, is much rarer and is used in events such as childbirth.
bullets: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable.
Negative feedback reverses a change.
Receptor, coordinator and effector form the control loop.
content.takeaway: Negative feedback pushes conditions back to the set point.

check.question: Which sequence describes negative feedback?
options: Stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response that reverses the change
Stimulus → effector → coordinator → receptor → response that increases the change
Receptor → stimulus → effector → coordinator → no response
Coordinator → receptor → stimulus → effector → response that increases the change
check.why: A receptor detects the stimulus, a coordinator processes it, and an effector reverses the change.

content.heading: Temperature regulation
paragraphs: Humans are endotherms, so they generate heat by metabolism and keep a core temperature near 37 °C. The hypothalamus acts as the thermostat, comparing blood temperature with the set point and triggering responses.

When the body is too hot, blood vessels in the skin widen (vasodilation), so more blood flows near the surface and heat is lost by radiation. Sweat glands release sweat, and evaporation cools the skin. Behaviour also helps: we seek shade and wear lighter clothes.

When the body is too cold, skin blood vessels narrow (vasoconstriction) to keep heat in, shivering muscles generate heat, and hair erects to trap a layer of air. Thyroxine and adrenaline raise the metabolic rate. Fever, which is a raised set point, helps fight infection.
bullets: Hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat.
Heat loss: vasodilation and sweating.
Heat gain: vasoconstriction, shivering and hair erection.
content.takeaway: Too hot: radiate and sweat. Too cold: conserve and shiver.

check.question: Which response helps cool the body on a hot day?
check.why: Vasodilation brings more blood to the skin surface and sweating adds evaporative cooling.

content.heading: Salt and water regulation
paragraphs: The kidneys control water and salt balance by filtering the blood and reabsorbing what the body needs. The amount of water reabsorbed depends on antidiuretic hormone (ADH), released from the posterior pituitary.

When the blood is too concentrated, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the change and trigger ADH release. ADH makes the collecting ducts of the kidney more permeable to water, so more water returns to the blood and the urine becomes small and concentrated.

When the blood is too dilute, ADH release falls and the kidneys excrete more dilute urine. Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex helps conserve sodium, and the sensation of thirst also drives water intake. This feedback keeps the tissue fluid at a suitable concentration.
bullets: Kidneys adjust water and salt reabsorption.
ADH increases water reabsorption and concentrates urine.
Aldosterone conserves sodium.
content.takeaway: ADH holds water back; aldosterone holds salt back.

check.question: A person sweats heavily and drinks little. What happens to ADH and urine?
options: ADH rises; urine becomes more concentrated
ADH rises; urine becomes more dilute
ADH falls; urine becomes more concentrated
ADH falls; urine becomes more dilute
check.why: Water loss concentrates the blood, so ADH rises and the kidneys reabsorb more water, producing concentrated urine.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Homeostasis uses negative feedback. The hypothalamus controls temperature, and the kidneys control water and salt with ADH and aldosterone. Vasodilation and sweating cool the body; vasoconstriction and shivering warm it.

content.problem: A worker spends a hot afternoon sweating heavily and drinks very little water. Explain how the body responds to conserve water.

steps.reason: Sweating removes water, so the blood becomes more concentrated.
steps.result: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus are stimulated.
steps.predictPrompt: Which hormone is released?

steps.reason: The posterior pituitary releases more antidiuretic hormone.
steps.result: The collecting ducts become more permeable to water.

steps.reason: More water is reabsorbed into the blood.
steps.result: Urine becomes small and concentrated, and thirst encourages drinking.

content.question: Why does a person produce more urine after drinking a large volume of water?
hints: Drinking water dilutes the blood.
Osmoreceptors detect the dilution and reduce ADH release.
Less ADH makes the collecting ducts less permeable to water.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting the Distribution of Organisms
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain how abiotic, edaphic and biotic factors determine where organisms live in Nigeria.

content.heading: Factors Affecting the Distribution of Organisms
paragraphs: During the harmattan dry season in Kano, farmers notice that pond fish crowd into the deepest part of the dugout as the water shrinks and warms.

content.heading: Abiotic Factors: Temperature, Rainfall and Altitude
paragraphs: Temperature controls enzyme activity and survival. Organisms with thick fur, fat layers or behavioural changes such as basking favour a warmer microclimate when temperatures fall. In cold highland areas, only species that tolerate low temperatures can survive and reproduce.

Rainfall, humidity and wind also shape distribution. Plants in wet southern Nigeria differ from those in the dry north, while wind spreads seeds and cools leaves during the dry season. A rain gauge measures rainfall, a thermometer measures temperature, and a hygrometer measures humidity.

Altitude changes temperature and rainfall together. As height increases, air becomes colder and thinner, so mountain crops and animals differ from lowland species. Organisms adapt through small size, thick coats, or timing of breeding to match the short cool season.
bullets: Thermometer: measures temperature in degrees Celsius
Rain gauge: measures amount of rainfall collected
Hygrometer: measures relative humidity of air
content.takeaway: Temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind and altitude limit survival and shape adaptation.

check.question: Which instrument is used to measure rainfall when studying distribution?
check.why: A rain gauge collects and measures rainfall, while a thermometer measures temperature and a hygrometer measures humidity.

content.heading: Water and Soil Factors: Salinity, Turbidity and pH
paragraphs: Salinity is the amount of dissolved salts in water. Freshwater fish die in salty sea water because osmosis removes water from their bodies. Estuaries where rivers meet the sea have changing salinity, so only tolerant species thrive there.

Turbidity measures how cloudy water is due to suspended particles. A Secchi disc lowered into water shows how far light penetrates, which affects photosynthesis by algae and eelgrass. Very turbid water in polluted rivers limits fish that need clear water.

Soil, or edaphic factors, include texture, water retention, air space, humus and pH. Sandy soil drains quickly and suits cassava, while clay soil holds water and suits rice. Soil pH affects nutrient availability, so acidic soil may favour pineapple while alkaline soil suits other crops.
bullets: Secchi disc: measures turbidity by depth of disappearance
pH meter: measures acidity or alkalinity of water and soil
Soil probe: measures moisture, texture and nutrient level
content.takeaway: Salinity, turbidity, pH and soil texture control which species survive in water and on land.

check.question: A Secchi disc is used to measure what?
check.why: A Secchi disc measures turbidity by how deep it remains visible in water.

content.heading: Biotic Factors and Human Activities
paragraphs: Biotic factors are living influences such as food, predators, disease and competition. A species may be absent from an area if its food is scarce or its predators too many. Competition removes resources, so the weaker species may move away or decline in number.

Human activities now shift distributions faster than climate alone. Farming, dams, urbanisation, pollution and deforestation destroy habitats and block movement. Zaadi rice farms at dams in northern Nigeria pull fish and water birds toward new wetlands, while Lake Chad shrinking forces species into smaller refuges.

During harmattan, dry winds and dust reduce water for plants and animals, so habitats contract. Pollution from factories and oil spills poisons water, while new roads and cities fragment forests. Conservation, reforestation and planned dams help species keep suitable habitat.
bullets: Food and disease: affect population size and spread
Predation and competition: remove or reduce a species locally
Dams and farms: create wetlands but flood old habitats
content.takeaway: Biotic pressures and human change move species, so conservation must protect food, habitat and movement routes.

check.question: Zaadi rice farms at dams mainly affect distribution by?
check.why: Zaadi farms at dams create shallow wetlands with food, attracting fish and water birds to a new habitat.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In JAMB questions, first decide whether the factor is abiotic, edaphic or biotic. Remember: temperature and rainfall are abiotic, soil texture is edaphic, and predation or competition is biotic.

content.problem: A Kano farmer finds fewer fish near the dam where water is very turbid, though algae feed is plentiful. What is limiting, and what should he test?

steps.operation: Identify the limiting factor from the scenario
steps.reason: Turbid water reduces light for algae and gills
steps.result: Turbidity, not food, is the main limit
steps.predictPrompt: What would a Secchi disc show here?

steps.reason: Secchi disc measures water clarity directly
steps.result: Lower Secchi disc depth means higher turbidity
steps.predictPrompt: What would you do if the depth is very shallow?

steps.operation: Suggest control of the human cause
steps.reason: Runoff and erosion raise turbidity in dams
steps.result: Plant grass strips and reduce soil erosion
steps.predictPrompt: How would clearer water help fish return?

content.question: Lake Chad is shrinking. Predict two abiotic and two biotic changes that will affect fish and water birds.
hints: Think rainfall and salinity
Think food and predation
Think human fishing and farming

lessons.title: Species Interactions
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to classify species interactions and predict their effects on populations.

content.heading: Species Interactions
paragraphs: At a Lagos market, a woman sells mistletoe growing on mango trees while her goat chews Loranthus leaves, and nearby a tapeworm treatment is advertised for livestock.

content.heading: Symbiosis: Mutualism, Commensalism and Parasitism
paragraphs: Symbiosis is a close living association between two species. In mutualism both partners benefit, as in lichen where fungus and algae live together. In commensalism one benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed.

Parasitism is when one organism, the parasite, benefits at the host's expense. A tapeworm inside a human intestine absorbs digested food, while head lice feed on blood and skin. Loranthus growing on a mango is a plant parasite that draws water and food from its host.

The key test is who gains and who loses. If both gain, it is mutualism; if only one gains and the other is unaffected, it is commensalism. If one gains and the other loses, it is parasitism, often with little or no benefit to the host.
bullets: Lichen: fungus and algae both gain
Barnacle on whale: barnacle gains, whale unaffected
Tapeworm in humans: worm gains, human loses
content.takeaway: Mutualism helps both, commensalism helps one only, and parasitism harms the host.

check.question: A butterfly visits a flower for nectar and pollinates it. The interaction is
check.why: Both gain: the butterfly gets nectar and the flower is pollinated, so it is mutualism.

content.heading: Predation, Competition, Cooperation and Amensalism
paragraphs: Predation is when one organism, the predator, kills and eats another, the prey. A leopard preying on grasscutters and a hawk catching chicks are examples. Predators check prey numbers and keep habitats in balance.

Competition is struggle for food, space or mates. Intra-specific competition is between members of the same species, while inter-specific competition is between different species. Both can reduce growth or push the weaker competitor out of the area.

Saprophytism is feeding on dead and decaying matter, as fungi and bacteria do. Cooperation is working together, as in ants guarding cattle egrets that remove ticks. Amensalism is when one is harmed and the other is unaffected, as Penicillium kills bacteria but gains nothing.
bullets: Saprophytes: fungi digest dead leaves and wood
Penicillium and bacteria: bacteria harmed, fungus unaffected
Hawks and mice: predator gains, prey loses
content.takeaway: Predation and competition reduce numbers, saprophytism recycles matter, and amensalism harms one side only.

check.question: Two goat species struggle for the same grass in one field. This is
check.why: Competition between different species is inter-specific competition.

content.heading: Classifying Unseen Examples in Exams
paragraphs: Read the scenario and ask who benefits and who is harmed. First check for feeding on dead matter, which points to saprophytism. Then check for killing and eating, which is predation, and for two species both losing from shared resources, which is competition.
Use the same test for symbiotic pairs. Lichen shows both partners gaining, so it is mutualism. A barnacle on a whale gains transport and food while the whale is unaffected, so it is commensalism.

Watch for amensalism and cooperation, which are often confused with other types. Amensalism harms one species while the other gains nothing, as with Penicillium and bacteria. Cooperation means both work together for a shared benefit, such as ants protecting insects that give sweet sap.
bullets: Both gain: mutualism
One gains, other unaffected: commensalism
One gains, other loses: parasitism or predation
content.takeaway: Ask who benefits, who is harmed, and whether feeding is on dead matter to classify correctly.

check.question: A barnacle on a whale, which gains transport, is
check.why: The barnacle gains while the whale is unaffected, which is commensalism.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If both organisms gain, choose mutualism; if one gains and the other is unaffected, choose commensalism. Parasitism always harms the host, so look for damage in the scenario carefully.

content.problem: Near a Lagos lagoon, a student sees lichen on a rock, a barnacle on a whale, and an orchid on a mango tree. Classify each pair.

steps.operation: Identify who benefits in each pair
steps.reason: Lichen both gain, barnacle gains only, orchid gains only
steps.result: Lichen mutualism, others commensalism
steps.predictPrompt: What extra clue would show parasitism?

steps.operation: Check if any organism is harmed
steps.reason: No harm to rock, whale or tree
steps.result: Commensalism fits both single-benefit pairs
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test for harm?

steps.reason: Both partners gain only in lichen
steps.result: Lichen mutualism, barnacle and orchid commensalism
steps.predictPrompt: Why is orchid not parasitism?

content.question: A fungus grows on dead wood and a bird eats ticks from a cattle's back. Name each interaction and give one reason.
hints: Dead wood means saprophytism
Think who benefits from tick removal
No harm means commensalism or cooperation

lessons.title: Food Chains, Webs and Trophic Levels
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain energy flow, food chains, food webs and trophic levels in Nigerian ecosystems.

content.heading: Food Chains, Webs and Trophic Levels
paragraphs: At a fish market in Calabar, smoked tilapia, grasscutter meat and garri are sold together, but in nature each of these foods comes from a different level of a food chain.

content.heading: Producers, Consumers and Decomposers
paragraphs: Green plants, algae and cyanobacteria are producers because they make food by photosynthesis. They form the first trophic level and support all other life. Herbivores such as grasscutters and tilapia eat producers and form the second trophic level.

Carnivores eat other animals and occupy higher levels. Primary carnivores eat herbivores, while secondary carnivores eat primary carnivores. Omnivores eat both plants and animals, as humans and crows do, so they can feed at more than one level.

Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead organisms and waste. They release nutrients back into soil and water for producers to use. Without decomposers, dead matter would pile up and nutrients would not be recycled for new growth.
bullets: Trophic level 1: producers make food
Trophic level 2: herbivores eat producers
Top carnivores: apex predators have few enemies
content.takeaway: Producers feed herbivores, herbivores feed carnivores, and decomposers recycle nutrients to producers.

check.question: In a food chain, the first trophic level is
check.why: Producers such as green plants make food by photosynthesis and form the first trophic level.

content.heading: Food Chains in Aquatic and Land Habitats
paragraphs: A food chain shows the flow of energy from one organism to the next. In water, algae are eaten by tilapia, and tilapia are eaten by the heron. Each arrow points from food to consumer, showing the direction of energy flow.

On land, grass is eaten by the grasscutter, which is eaten by the leopard. A longer chain might start with leaves, go to a caterpillar, then to a small bird, and finally to a hawk. Chains are rarely long because energy is lost at each step.

Most organisms feed on more than one type of food, so chains link together into food webs. A web shows alternative feeding routes and helps communities survive when one food source fails. Exams often test whether you can draw arrows from food to eater.
bullets: Algae to tilapia to heron: aquatic chain
Grass to grasscutter to leopard: land chain
Arrow direction: from food to consumer
content.takeaway: Food chains are straight lines of energy flow, while food webs link many chains together.

check.question: In a food chain diagram, arrows point
check.why: Arrows show energy flow from food to consumer, so they point from food to eater.

content.heading: Energy Loss, Pyramids and Decomposers
paragraphs: At each trophic level, most energy is lost as heat, movement and waste. Only about ten percent passes to the next level, a pattern called the ten percent law. This is why there are many producers but few top carnivores.

Pyramids show this balance. A pyramid of numbers has many producers and fewer consumers at each higher level. A pyramid of biomass shows total mass, which is usually large for producers and small for large carnivores, though aquatic pyramids can look different.

Decomposers close the cycle by breaking down dead producers and consumers. Their enzymes release minerals that roots and algae absorb again. Without decomposers, nutrients stay locked in dead matter and producers would soon run out of food.
bullets: Ten percent law: little energy reaches top levels
Pyramid of numbers: many producers, few predators
Pyramid of biomass: total mass falls with level
content.takeaway: Energy falls to about ten percent per level, so pyramids narrow and decomposers recycle nutrients.

check.question: According to the ten percent law, about how much energy passes to the next level?
check.why: Only about ten percent of energy passes to the next trophic level, so pyramids narrow quickly.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Draw arrows from food to eater, never the reverse. Remember the ten percent law explains why chains are short and why pyramids of numbers are broad at the base.

content.problem: A Niger Delta pond has algae, tilapia, and a heron. The pond also has a small snake that eats fish. Build the chain and web.

steps.reason: Algae make food, tilapia eat algae, heron eats tilapia
steps.result: Chain algae to tilapia to heron
steps.predictPrompt: What if snake adds another route?

steps.reason: Snake also eats fish, so fish have two predators
steps.result: Web shows fish eaten by heron and snake
steps.predictPrompt: How does web help ecosystem?

steps.reason: Energy drops at each level
steps.result: Pyramid narrows toward heron and snake
steps.predictPrompt: Why are there fewer herons than tilapia?

content.question: Explain why a food web is more stable than a single food chain in a Nigerian forest.
hints: Think alternative food sources
Think predators and prey
Think what happens when one species declines

lessons.title: Carbon, Water and Nitrogen Cycles
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to describe the carbon, water and nitrogen cycles and explain human effects on them.

content.heading: Carbon, Water and Nitrogen Cycles
paragraphs: In a rice farm near Kano, children watch rain fill the dam, plants grow green, and cattle return dung to the soil, all showing water, carbon and nitrogen moving in cycles.

content.heading: The Carbon Cycle and Global Warming
paragraphs: Plants take in carbon dioxide and use it in photosynthesis to make glucose. Animals eat plants and release carbon dioxide during respiration. Respiration and decomposition return carbon dioxide to the air, keeping a balance of carbon and oxygen.

Burning wood, coal and petrol, called combustion, also releases carbon dioxide. Deforestation and fossil fuel use raise carbon dioxide faster than plants can absorb it. Extra carbon dioxide traps heat in the air, causing global warming and changing rainfall patterns.

The ocean acts as a large carbon sink when carbonates form in shells and sink. Some carbon is stored in limestone and fossil fuels for millions of years. Protecting forests and reducing burning helps keep the carbon and oxygen balance stable.
bullets: Photosynthesis: uses carbon dioxide, releases oxygen
Respiration and combustion: release carbon dioxide
Ocean sink: stores carbon as carbonate shells
content.takeaway: Photosynthesis, respiration, combustion and decomposition cycle carbon, while oceans store some long term.

check.question: Which processes release carbon dioxide into the air?
check.why: Respiration, combustion and decomposition return carbon dioxide to the air, while photosynthesis uses it.

content.heading: The Water Cycle and Climate
paragraphs: Water evaporates from oceans, lakes and rivers under the sun. Plants also release water vapour through transpiration from their leaves. Together, evaporation and transpiration lift water into the air as an invisible vapour.

As warm air rises, vapour cools and condenses into clouds. Water falls as precipitation, such as rain, which is common in southern Nigeria. Some rain soaks into soil as groundwater, while the rest runs off the surface into streams and rivers.

The cycle moves water continuously, so the amount on Earth stays almost constant. Deforestation reduces transpiration and runoff patterns, which can make rainfall less regular. The water cycle therefore affects climate, farming and the availability of clean water.
bullets: Evaporation and transpiration: lift water to air
Condensation and precipitation: form clouds and rain
Runoff and groundwater: move water to rivers and wells
content.takeaway: Evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff and groundwater move water through the environment.

check.question: Transpiration is the process by which plants
check.why: Transpiration releases water vapour from leaves into the air, part of the water cycle.

content.heading: The Nitrogen Cycle and Legume Crops
paragraphs: Plants need nitrogen to make proteins, but most cannot use nitrogen gas from air. Fixation converts nitrogen gas into usable compounds. Rhizobium bacteria in legume roots, free-living Azotobacter, and lightning all fix nitrogen for crops.

Nitrification turns ammonium into nitrites and then nitrates, which plants absorb easily. Nitrosomonas acts first, then Nitrobacter completes the change. Animal waste and urea break down to ammonium, feeding nitrification and keeping nitrogen available in soil.

Denitrification returns nitrates to nitrogen gas and completes the cycle. Pseudomonas bacteria carry out denitrification in waterlogged, airless soil. Farmers use leguminous crops such as groundnut and cowpea in rotation to restore nitrogen and reduce fertiliser needs.
bullets: Fixation: Rhizobium, Azotobacter and lightning fix nitrogen
Nitrification: Nitrosomonas then Nitrobacter make nitrates
Denitrification: Pseudomonas returns nitrogen gas to air
content.takeaway: Fixation, nitrification and denitrification move nitrogen between air, soil and plants for protein making.

check.question: In nitrification, Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter convert ammonium to
check.why: Nitrosomonas and then Nitrobacter convert ammonium into nitrites and then nitrates for plant uptake.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For nitrogen questions, remember the order: fixation, then nitrification by Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter, then plant uptake, and finally denitrification by Pseudomonas back to nitrogen gas in the air for exam.

content.problem: A Kano farmer grows millet alone every year and yields fall. He adds cowpea in rotation and returns cattle waste. Explain the change using the nitrogen cycle.

steps.reason: Continuous millet removes nitrates without replacement
steps.result: Soil nitrogen falls and yields drop
steps.predictPrompt: What would fixation add?

steps.reason: Legume roots fix nitrogen gas into soil
steps.result: More nitrates form through nitrification
steps.predictPrompt: What role do manure bacteria play?

steps.reason: Waste breaks down to ammonium then nitrates
steps.result: Plants absorb nitrates and grow better
steps.predictPrompt: How does denitrification complete the cycle?

content.question: How would deforestation and burning in northern Nigeria change the carbon and water cycles together?
hints: Think carbon dioxide release
Think transpiration and rainfall
Think soil erosion and runoff

lessons.title: Aquatic Habitats
lessons.objective: Learners will describe aquatic adaptations in Nigerian ponds, rivers and mangroves.

content.heading: Aquatic Habitats
paragraphs: A student in Awka watches tilapia jump near water lilies in a village pond during the rains and wonders where fish and insects hide.

content.heading: Ponds and Lakes: Still Water Communities
paragraphs: Ponds and lakes hold stagnant water that warms easily under the Nigerian sun. Sunlight penetrates only a few metres, so most life stays near the surface. Stagnant conditions also lower dissolved oxygen, especially in deep or polluted water.

Tiny phytoplankton drift near the surface and multiply during the rainy season. Water lilies root in muddy beds while their broad leaves shade the water below. Tilapia feed on plankton, plants and small invertebrates in these warm layers.

Frogs, snails, mosquito larvae and dragonfly nymphs complete the food web in ponds. Farmers often dig ponds near Awka and Onitsha to breed tilapia for food. Seasonal flooding connects small ponds to streams, bringing in nutrients and new colonists.
bullets: Phytoplankton form the base of the food chain in ponds and lakes.
Water lilies provide food and shelter but can trap debris in still water.
Tilapia tolerate warm, low-oxygen water better than many native fish.
content.takeaway: Still ponds are layered systems where plankton, plants and tilapia depend on light and oxygen.

check.question: What forms the food base in ponds?
check.why: Plankton photosynthesise food for small animals.

content.heading: Streams and Rivers: Life in Flowing Water
paragraphs: Streams and rivers carry flowing water that is usually well mixed and rich in dissolved oxygen. Riffles, where water splashes over stones, add oxygen rapidly as currents tumble. Rapid flow also prevents stagnant warming and algal scum common in ponds.

In shallow riffles, insect larvae cling to smooth stones to avoid being swept downstream. Fish such as catfish and tilapia hunt insects, leaves and fallen fruits carried by the current. Freshwater crabs shelter under rocks and scavenge dead organisms.

During the rainy season, rivers flood nearby lowlands and deposit fertile mud. Market gardeners in Ibadan use flood plains to grow yams and vegetables. Fishermen cast nets in calm pools where oxygen remains high and food is plentiful.
bullets: Flowing water supplies a steady supply of dissolved oxygen for animals.
Riffles aerate water and support oxygen-loving insect larvae and fish.
Flood plains enrich soil and provide breeding grounds for fish.
content.takeaway: Flowing rivers stay oxygen rich, so riffles favour insects and fish that need fresh water.

check.question: Why do larvae live in riffles?
check.why: Riffles add oxygen needed by larvae.

content.heading: Seashores and Mangrove Swamps
paragraphs: Seashores along the Lagos coast experience daily tides that alternately flood and expose sand and mud. Intertidal zones endure strong waves, changing salinity and drying in the hot sun. Animals here must tolerate salty water and survive without it for hours.

Mangrove swamps in the Niger Delta grow in soft, oxygen-poor mud under brackish water. Red mangroves send arching prop roots to support trees and trap sediments near the water. Black mangroves push cone-like pneumatophores upward to take in air at low tide.

Fiddler crabs, snails and juvenile fish use mangrove roots as shelter and feeding grounds. Salt tolerance helps these animals pump out excess salt and retain fresh water. Oyster beds and mudskippers also prosper in the damp, sheltered swamp margins.
bullets: Tides shape seashore life by sorting animals into wet and dry zones.
Prop roots support mangroves while pneumatophores allow roots to breathe.
Crabs and fish survive salinity changes through specialised salt control.
content.takeaway: Tides and salty mud demand roots that breathe and animals that control salt.

check.question: What do pneumatophores do?
check.why: They rise from mud to absorb air.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In JAMB questions, link each habitat to its water movement and oxygen level. Remember: still ponds favour plankton, riffles favour insects, and mangroves favour salt control. Highlight these contrasts for quick revision.

content.problem: A Delta fisherman catches crabs in mangrove roots at low tide. Explain why.

steps.reason: Mud and roots exposed
steps.result: Crabs hide and feed

steps.reason: Fish enter with seawater
steps.result: Fish feed near roots

steps.reason: Salt and oxygen needs differ
steps.result: Fishers follow tide

content.question: Where do Lagos crabs hide at low tide?
hints: Exposed mud
Mangrove roots
Salt control

lessons.title: Terrestrial and Arboreal Habitats
lessons.objective: Learners will describe land adaptations in Nigerian savanna, canopy and soil.

content.heading: Terrestrial and Arboreal Habitats
paragraphs: On a farm outside Jos, a boy watches grasscutters dart into tall grass as a harmattan wind spreads dry leaves changing colour.

content.heading: Savanna Grassland and Abandoned Farmland
paragraphs: Savanna grasslands around Bida and Ogbomosho receive seasonal rain followed by a long dry season. Deep-rooted grasses, such as elephant grass, survive drought and recover quickly after fire. Farmers often abandon old fields where grasses and shrubs reclaim the soil naturally.

Fire adaptation is essential because dry-season bush fires sweep the savanna each year. Thick underground stems and waxy leaves protect buds from heat and reduce water loss. After burning, fresh green shoots emerge to feed grazers and attract insects.

Grasscutters hide in dense tufts and feed on tender shoots during the rainy months. Birds such as francolins hunt seeds while reptiles bask on warm laterite soils. In abandoned farmland, shrubs and small trees trap soil and restore moisture for new crops.
bullets: Grasses dominate savanna because deep roots store water and resist fire.
Fire removes dead litter and triggers fresh growth for grazers.
Grasscutters and birds depend on grass cover for food and shelter.
content.takeaway: Savanna grasses persist through drought and fire, feeding grasscutters and other animals.

check.question: What helps grasses survive fire?
check.why: Underground buds regrow after fire.

content.heading: Arboreal Life in the Tree Tops
paragraphs: Arboreal animals live in the canopy of trees in forests and savanna woodlands. Monkeys swing through branches near Zaria, grasping limbs with hands and feet. Their long tails aid balance while they forage on fruits, leaves and insects.

Birds such as hornbills and weavers nest high in branches where ground predators cannot reach. Weavers build hanging nests that sway safely in the wind. Canopy density provides shade, food and escape routes throughout the year.

Ants and termites form large colonies in tree forks and under bark. Their activity supports arboreal food webs by recycling dead wood and leaves. Study canopy life to understand food, shelter and safety in the treetops.
bullets: Monkeys use grasping limbs and tails to move safely among branches.
Weaver birds build hanging nests high above ground predators.
Ants and termites recycle organic matter within the canopy.
content.takeaway: Canopy life offers food and safety, but needs limbs and nests for life aloft.

check.question: Why build nests high in trees?
check.why: High nests avoid ground predators.

content.heading: Burrow Life Beneath the Soil
paragraphs: Burrowing animals live in tunnels dug into soil, where temperature and moisture change slowly. Earthworms eat decaying leaves and loosen the soil for roots. Burrows also protect animals from harmattan heat, wind and heavy rain.

Termites build mounds with well-planned chambers that trap cool air and store food. Their colonies regulate humidity so fungal gardens can grow inside the nest walls. In Nigeria, termites often fill soil with tunnels from farms to forest edges.

Other soil animals such as millipedes, beetles and burrowing frogs feed on litter. Their burrows let water soak in and prevent soil flooding during storms. Farmers favour these organisms because they improve soil structure and aeration for crops.
bullets: Earthworms aerate soil and enrich it with nutrient-rich casts.
Termite mounds control temperature and humidity for the colony.
Burrows guard animals from drought, heat and sudden rain.
content.takeaway: Underground burrows keep soil animals cool, moist and safe from weather.

check.question: How do burrows help dry-season worms?
check.why: Burrows stay cool and damp.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: JAMB often pairs habitat with adaptation. For savanna write fire and drought, for canopy write grip and nests, and for burrows write moisture and temperature shelter during their harsh seasons now.

content.problem: A Jos farmer finds fewer grasscutters after fire. Explain effects.

steps.reason: Food and shelter gone
steps.result: Grasscutters decline

steps.reason: Worms hide underground
steps.result: Soil animals survive

steps.reason: Fruits remain in trees
steps.result: Monkeys suffer less

content.question: Where are Ibadan worms after rain?
hints: Damp soil
Feeding habits
Burrow depth

lessons.title: Tropical Rainforest of Nigeria
lessons.objective: Learners will explain rainforest location and layered structure in southern Nigeria.

content.heading: Tropical Rainforest of Nigeria
paragraphs: In Calabar, heavy rain falls almost every afternoon while tall trees drip and leaves glisten in cool shade under thick clouds.

content.heading: Location and Rainfall in the South
paragraphs: Nigeria's tropical rainforest grows in the south where annual rainfall exceeds 2000 mm. States such as Cross River, Ondo and Rivers receive the heaviest rain each year. Rain falls in most months across southern Nigeria, leaving only a short dry season.

The Niger Delta and southern uplands sit under constant moist air from the Atlantic. High humidity favours rapid leaf growth and thick plant cover throughout the year. Frequent rainfall leaches nutrients from surface soils, leaving poor, acidic conditions for crops.

Laterite soils dominate under rainforest, as iron and aluminium remain after heavy leaching. Farmers terrace steep slopes to protect this fragile soil from erosion. Conservation of laterite areas preserves water quality and wildlife corridors for towns and farms downstream.
bullets: Rainfall over 2000 mm creates warm, wet conditions for rainforest growth.
Southern states and the Niger Delta host the main forest belt.
Laterite soils are acidic and nutrient-poor due to leaching.
content.takeaway: Heavy southern rainfall and laterite soils shape Nigeria's rainforest climate.

check.question: What rainfall fits rainforest?
check.why: Rainforest exceeds 2000 mm yearly.

content.heading: Forest Layers and Rich Diversity
paragraphs: Emergent trees rise above the canopy, reaching 40 metres in fertile lowland areas across southern Nigeria. Their tough leaves resist strong winds and occasional dry spells during harmattan. Buttress roots spread wide at the base to support these giants safely.

Below emergents lies the closed canopy of tall trees, where leaves form a green roof. Lianas climb through gaps to reach sunlight and flower at treetops. The canopy layers trap moisture and create cool, still conditions underneath.

The understorey holds shrubs, saplings and herbs that tolerate deep shade and moisture. Gorillas, seed-eating birds and crickets shelter among dense undergrowth nearby. Nigeria's rainforest holds rich diversity because layered plants supply food and habitat vertically.
bullets: Emergent trees and buttress roots support the forest ceiling.
Lianas link canopy to understorey and boost plant diversity.
Understorey shade shelters many small animals and young plants.
content.takeaway: Layered rainforest supports diverse life from canopy to forest floor.

check.question: What do buttress roots do?
check.why: They anchor tall trees on land.

content.heading: Swamp Forest, Threats and Conservation
paragraphs: Niger Delta swamp forest grows in waterlogged soils beside creeks and rivers across southern wetlands. Raffia palms and short mangroves dominate where brackish water meets fresh water daily. Crabs, fish and snails thrive in this rich, flooded environment with organised feeding behaviour.

Deforestation for palm oil plantations, logging and farming now threatens the rainforest. Settlers clear forest rapidly for cocoa and rubber estates near Lagos. Plantation farms often replace diverse forest with single crops that need chemicals.

Conservation now protects remnants through national parks and organised community reserves. Sustainable farming restores buffers of fast-growing trees around degraded areas for wildlife. JAMB favours questions on swamp adaptation and on why forest loss harms climate.
bullets: Swamp forest tolerates flooding and brackish water in the Delta.
Plantations and logging drive rapid rainforest loss in the south.
Parks and reserves conserve species and moderate local climate.
content.takeaway: Delta swamp forests need protection from plantations and logging pressure.

check.question: What most threatens rainforest?
check.why: Plantations clear forests for crops.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Remember the north to south rainfall gradient. JAMB links rainforest to over 2000 mm, laterite soils, buttress roots and high diversity in layered trees to answer Nigerian context questions fast.

content.problem: A Cross River group finds roots and lianas. What to record?

steps.reason: Tall trees exceed canopy
steps.result: Note root support

steps.reason: Need light to flower
steps.result: Link climbing diversity

steps.reason: Shrubs grow below canopy
steps.result: Record moisture needs

content.question: Why Delta swamp not savanna?
hints: Heavy rainfall
Waterlogged soils
Laterite leaching

lessons.title: Savanna, Desert and Highland Biomes
lessons.objective: Learners will compare Nigerian savanna, desert oases and highland grasslands.

content.heading: Savanna, Desert and Highland Biomes
paragraphs: Travelling north from Abuja in harmattan season, grasses shrink, dunes appear, then misty plateaus rise where air feels cool at night.

content.heading: Guinea Savanna of the Middle Belt
paragraphs: Guinea savanna occupies the middle belt with 1000 to 1500 mm of annual rainfall. Tall grass grows 1 to 3 metres high during the rainy months. Trees such as Isoberlinia and Parkia dot the grassland and drop leaves in the dry season.

The burn regime helps Guinea savanna maintain open grassland against encroaching forest. Yearly fires clear litter, kill pests and recycle nutrients into soil. Farmers burn before the first rains to encourage fresh shoots for livestock.

Shea, locust bean and dawadawa trees offer nuts and food for families. Antelopes, guinea fowl and grasscutters shelter in the tall grass during rains. JAMB often asks about burn timing and how fire favours grasses over trees.
bullets: Guinea savanna receives 1000 to 1500 mm and tall grass 1 to 3 metres.
Isoberlinia and Parkia trees adapt to seasonal fire and drought.
Burn regime clears litter and favours grasses over shrubs.
content.takeaway: Guinea savanna blends tall grass, Isoberlinia parkland and yearly fire.

check.question: How tall is Guinea grass?
check.why: Grasses reach 1 to 3 metres in rains.

content.heading: Sudan Savanna and the Sahel Edge
paragraphs: Sudan savanna covers the north with less than 1000 mm of rainfall each year. Short grasses, often under 1 metre, grow in scattered clumps between trees. The dry season lasts six to seven months under hazy harmattan skies.

Shea and baobab trees survive drought with deep roots and thick trunks that store water. Glaucous leaves reduce water loss while seeds remain dormant through dry spells. This zone is a tsetse-free area because dry air limits the fly.

Farmers in Kano and Katsina grow millet, sorghum and groundnuts with short seasonal crops. Nomadic herders move south in the dry season seeking fresh pasture. Sudan savanna shows adaptation to fierce sun and low moisture year after year.
bullets: Sudan savanna has under 1000 mm rain and short, sparse grass.
Shea and baobab store water to survive long dry seasons.
Tsetse-free dry air supports cattle rearing in the north.
content.takeaway: Sudan savanna shows tree adaptations to low rain and intense sun.

check.question: How do shea trees survive drought?
check.why: Trunks store water for drought.

content.heading: Desert Oases and Highland Grasslands
paragraphs: The extreme north-east holds desert with less than 250 mm of annual rainfall. Active dunes shift with wind near Borno, while xerophytes survive with tiny leaves and succulent stems. Date palms cluster around oases where underground water reaches the surface.

Highland biomes rise in cool mists on the Jos Plateau and Obudu Plateau Cross River. Mambilla Plateau adds another cool grassland where fog lowers temperature. These oases of temperate climate stand out from hot lowlands.

Jos Plateau grows potatoes and Irish crops that need cool nights and mist. Highland grasses support cattle and attract tourists to viewpoints and canyons. Highland mist supplies moisture to crops that fail in surrounding savanna heat.
bullets: Desert xerophytes cut water loss with small leaves and coatings.
Oases allow desert farming where water reaches the surface.
Highland grasslands enjoy mist and temperate climate for crops.
content.takeaway: Desert oases and misty highlands contrast sharply with hot savanna plains.

check.question: Why suit Irish potatoes on Jos Plateau?
check.why: Mist keeps highland climate temperate.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Learn biomes from south to north. Pair Guinea savanna with 1000 to 1500 mm, Sudan with under 1000 mm, desert under 250 mm and highlands with mist for ridge revision.

content.problem: A trader moves Kano sorghum to Jos and sees frost. Explain why.

steps.reason: Kano is hot and dry
steps.result: Jos is cool and misty

steps.reason: Highland air cools
steps.result: Frost harms sorghum

steps.reason: Potatoes suit cool soils
steps.result: Plant temperate crops

content.question: How tell Guinea from Sudan savanna?
hints: Rainfall amount
Grass height
Tree species

lessons.title: Population Density and Size
lessons.objective: Measure population density and explain factors that determine the size of a population in an ecosystem.

content.heading: Population Density and Size
paragraphs: At the University of Ibadan botanical garden, Adebayo counts wild yam seedlings along a shady path. He wonders whether they are crowded or sparse, and how ecologists compare such counts fairly across different places.

content.heading: What Population Density Means
paragraphs: Population density is the number of individuals of a species within a given unit area or volume. It shows whether a species is crowded or thinly spread in its habitat.

Counting every individual is often impossible in a large forest or field. Ecologists sample a small representative part with a quadrat, usually a 1 m² frame placed at random points. Where plants are spread widely, they lay a transect line and sample quadrats along it.

Density is the total count divided by the total sampled area. If 40 yam seedlings are found in four 1 m² quadrats, the density is 40 ÷ 4 = 10 seedlings per m². Sampling must be random and repeated so results represent the whole area.
bullets: Density = total number counted ÷ total area sampled
A quadrat is a 1 m² frame; a transect is a line along which quadrats are sampled
Random placement and repetition improve accuracy and fairness
content.takeaway: Density tells how crowded a species is per unit area, estimated by quadrat sampling.

check.question: A student counts 60 seedlings in six 1 m² quadrats. What is the density?
check.why: Density = 60 ÷ 6 = 10 seedlings per square metre.

content.heading: Factors That Affect Population Size
paragraphs: Biotic factors are living or once-living factors that affect a population. Abundant food, low predation and good reproductive ability allow populations to grow quickly. Pests, disease, competition and predation reduce numbers by lowering survival and reproduction.

Abiotic factors are non-living conditions such as temperature, light, water, space and pH. Each species has an optimum range, and harsh conditions lower its density in the soil. For example, yam seedlings grow poorly when water is scarce or soil pH is too acidic.

No factor acts alone, and populations usually settle near the carrying capacity of their habitat. When food or space runs out, competition increases and density falls. Ecologists therefore measure both biotic and abiotic factors when explaining population changes.
bullets: Biotic factors: food, pests, disease, predation, competition and reproductive ability
Abiotic factors: temperature, light, water, space and soil pH
Optimum conditions favour growth; unfavourable conditions reduce density
content.takeaway: Population size depends on living and non-living factors that affect survival and reproduction.

check.question: Which set lists only abiotic factors affecting population size?
check.why: Temperature, light and water are non-living conditions, so they are abiotic.

content.heading: Overcrowding in Human Populations
paragraphs: Overcrowding means too many people living in an area for its resources and services. It is often caused by a high birth rate and a falling death rate. Good healthcare, sanitation and nutrition keep more children alive, so numbers rise.

Overcrowding puts pressure on food, water, space, housing and jobs. It spreads disease quickly, causes unemployment and creates slums with poor sanitation. Schools, hospitals and roads become congested and fierce competition for resources increases within the community.

Control measures include family planning education, girls' education and child healthcare programmes. Investment in housing, jobs, clean water and farming improves living standards. Such measures slow growth without coercion and improve quality of life.
bullets: Causes: high birth rate, falling death rate and better healthcare
Effects: disease, unemployment, slums and pressure on food and space
Control: family planning, education and improved housing and services
content.takeaway: Overcrowding strains resources and services, so planning and education help control it.

check.question: Which is a direct consequence of overcrowding in cities?
options: More space and food per person
check.why: Overcrowding spreads disease and pressures jobs, housing, food and space, leading to slums.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In JAMB questions, density is always number divided by area. Write the unit, such as individuals per square metre, and check whether biotic factors are living while abiotic factors are non-living before choosing an option.

content.problem: At a primary school garden in Enugu, Chiamaka places four 1 m² quadrats along a transect and counts 36 pawpaw seedlings. Calculate the density and explain what the result suggests.

steps.operation: Add the seedlings in all quadrats: 36
steps.reason: Density uses the total count from the sampled area
steps.result: Total count = 36 seedlings

steps.operation: Add the sampled area: 4 × 1 m² = 4 m²
steps.reason: Each quadrat covers 1 m², so four quadrats cover 4 m²
steps.result: Sampled area = 4 m²

steps.operation: Divide total count by total area: 36 ÷ 4
steps.reason: Density is number per unit area
steps.result: Density = 9 seedlings per m²

content.question: A farmer in Kano counts 50 millet plants in five 1 m² quadrats. Is the density high or low, and which factor would you check first to explain it?
hints: Divide 50 by the total area
Think of food, water and pests
Consider temperature and rainfall too

lessons.title: Competition and Niche
lessons.objective: Explain intra-specific and inter-specific competition and how niche differentiation reduces competition in an ecosystem.

content.heading: Competition and Niche
paragraphs: On a farm near Zaria, sorghum grows taller than Striga hiding among its roots. The farmer wonders why the crop is stunted. This lesson explains how competition for resources shapes the growth of plants and animals.

content.heading: Intra-specific Competition
paragraphs: Intra-specific competition occurs between members of the same species. Their needs are almost identical, so they compete strongly for the same resources. This competition is usually intense because individuals want the same food, mates, space, light and water.

In plants, seedlings of one species shade one another and compete for light, water and mineral salts. In animals, males compete for mates and territories, while all individuals compete for food and shelter. The strongest individuals survive and reproduce, passing on their genes.

Intra-specific competition limits population size and density in a habitat. When resources are scarce, growth slows, reproduction falls and some individuals die. It therefore helps to keep a population near what the environment can support in a crowded habitat.
bullets: Same species, same needs: food, mates, space, light and water
Plants compete for light, water and mineral salts
Strongest individuals survive; density is limited
content.takeaway: Intra-specific competition is contest within a species for identical resources needed for survival.

check.question: Two male goats fight for access to females during the mating season. This is an example of
check.why: Both are males of the same species competing for mates, so it is intra-specific.

content.heading: Inter-specific Competition
paragraphs: Inter-specific competition occurs between different species that need the same resource. One species may gain while the other loses, or both may suffer. This competition is less direct than intra-specific competition, but it can still reduce growth and yield.

Striga is a parasitic weed that grows on sorghum roots and steals water and nutrients. In millet and groundnut mixtures, one crop may shade the other or use water faster. Farmers therefore space crops well and remove weeds early to reduce this loss.

Where two species compete strongly, the better adapted species often replaces the weaker one. This replacement changes the composition of the community over time. Understanding the contest helps farmers and ecologists predict crop yields in the field.
bullets: Different species competing for the same food, water or light
Striga steals water and nutrients from sorghum roots
Millet and groundnut compete when spaced too closely together
content.takeaway: Inter-specific competition is contest between species, and the better adapted may dominate.

check.question: Striga growing on sorghum roots and reducing its growth is an example of
check.why: Sorghum and Striga are different species competing for the same water and nutrients.

content.heading: Niche Differentiation and Succession
paragraphs: A niche is the role and position of a species in its ecosystem, including how it obtains food and space. When species partition resources, they use them differently, so competition falls. For example, birds may feed at different heights on the same tree.

Partitioning also happens through timing and root depth in plants. One species may grow in the rainy season while another grows later, or roots may occupy shallow and deep soil layers. Each species then obtains enough resources to survive and reproduce.

Competition drives succession as pioneers are replaced by better competitors. Early species modify the soil and shade, allowing shrubs and later trees to invade. Over time, the community changes from pioneer to climax species in a stable environment.
bullets: Niche: feeding height, timing of growth and root depth
Sharing resources differently reduces competition between species
Competition drives replacement of pioneers by climax species
content.takeaway: Niche differentiation reduces competition by partitioning resources among species in a habitat.

check.question: Two bird species feed at different heights on the same tree. This shows
check.why: Feeding at different heights partitions food, so each species uses the tree differently.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: JAMB often asks whether competition is within one species or between species. Look for the phrase same species for intra-specific and different species for inter-specific. Remember that niche partitioning reduces competition between species.

content.problem: In a school farm at Jos, 20 millet seedlings and 20 groundnut seedlings compete for water in the same bed. After one month, millet is taller and groundnut is stunted. Explain the type of competition and the result.

steps.operation: Identify the competing organisms: millet and groundnut
steps.reason: They are different species needing the same water and light
steps.result: Competition is inter-specific

steps.operation: Compare growth: millet taller, groundnut stunted
steps.reason: Millet obtained more water and light than groundnut
steps.result: Millet outcompeted groundnut

steps.reason: The better adapted species will dominate the bed
steps.result: Groundnut density and yield will fall

content.question: Two bird species feed on the same tree but at different heights. Is this competition, niche differentiation, or succession, and why?
hints: Think of how they partition food
Consider feeding height on the tree
Succession requires change over time

lessons.title: Ecological Succession
lessons.objective: Describe the stages of primary and secondary succession and explain the features of a climax community.

content.heading: Ecological Succession
paragraphs: After a landslide near Idanre exposes bare rock, local farmers watch hardy lichens appear first. Over many years, green plants and trees return. This lesson traces how one community replaces another until it becomes stable and mature.

content.heading: Primary Succession on Bare Rock
paragraphs: Primary succession begins on a bare area where no soil exists, such as exposed rock or cooled lava. It starts slowly because organisms must create the conditions for others to live. The first organisms are pioneers that can survive harsh, dry surfaces with little water and no nutrients.

Lichens break down rock and form a thin layer of soil, then mosses grow and add more humus. Herbs and grasses grow thicker, shrubs follow, and finally trees form a forest. Each stage builds soil that improves water holding and nutrient supply.

The sequence is lichens, then mosses, herbs, shrubs and forest, and it may take many years. Soil becomes deeper, darker and richer as roots and dead organisms accumulate. Small animals and fungi arrive as the habitat becomes sheltered and moist.
bullets: Bare rock: lichens first, then mosses and herbs
Shrubs and trees follow as soil builds up
Each stage improves soil for the next stage
content.takeaway: Primary succession moves from bare rock to forest as pioneers build soil gradually.

check.question: What is the correct order in primary succession on bare rock?
check.why: Lichens colonise rock first and build soil, then mosses, herbs, shrubs and forest follow.

content.heading: Secondary Succession on Cleared Farmland
paragraphs: Secondary succession begins where soil already exists, such as cleared farmland or a harvested forest. Seeds, roots and soil organisms remain, so colonisation is faster. Pioneer grasses and small herbs appear within weeks, not years.

Grasses build cover and add humus, then shrubs and young trees grow rapidly. Because soil is already present, water and nutrients are available from the start. This gives secondary succession a higher net primary productivity, or NPP, than primary succession.

Human clearing often resets land to the grass stage, and farming may repeat the cycle. If land is abandoned, succession continues towards shrubs and forest. The speed depends on nearby seed sources, rainfall and soil quality in the area.
bullets: Cleared farmland retains soil, seeds and roots
Grasses and herbs appear first and grow fast
Higher NPP because soil and nutrients remain
content.takeaway: Secondary succession is faster than primary because soil and seed sources remain.

check.question: Why is secondary succession faster than primary succession?
options: Soil, seeds and roots remain after clearing
Bare rock builds soil very quickly
Lichens are absent in secondary succession
check.why: Cleared farmland still has soil and seed sources, so grasses and shrubs establish quickly.

content.heading: Climax Community and Resetting Factors
paragraphs: A climax community is the final, stable stage of succession in an area under the local climate. It is diverse, mature and self-perpetuating because its species can regenerate themselves. Large trees, many animals and a deep leaf litter characterise such a community.

In Nigeria, the Omo Forest in Ogun State and Yankari Game Reserve in Bauchi State show climax-like communities. Omo Forest supports tall trees, primates and diverse plants, while Yankari has stable savanna woodland and many wildlife species. These communities resist small changes.

Fire, farming and drought can reset succession by removing plants and soil cover. Fire clears shrubs and returns land to grasses, while farming clears trees for crops. After such disturbance, succession begins again from an early stage.
bullets: Climax: stable, diverse and self-perpetuating community
Examples: Omo Forest climax and Yankari woodland
Fire, farming and drought reset succession
content.takeaway: A climax community is stable and diverse, but fire, farming or drought can reset it.

check.question: Which feature best describes a climax community?
check.why: A climax community is mature, diverse and able to maintain itself under local conditions.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In JAMB, primary succession starts on bare rock while secondary starts where soil remains. List the order lichens, mosses, herbs, shrubs then forest, and remember climax communities are stable and diverse until fire, farming or drought resets them.

content.problem: A landslide near Abeokuta exposes bare rock, while a nearby farm is abandoned after harvest. Which area will become forested faster, and why? Give the pioneer organisms for the faster area.

steps.operation: Compare starting conditions: rock has no soil, farm has soil and seeds
steps.reason: Soil supplies water, nutrients and a site for roots
steps.result: Farm will succeed faster

steps.reason: Grasses and small herbs colonise cleared soil quickly
steps.result: Pioneers: grasses and herbs

steps.reason: Lichens must build soil before larger plants grow
steps.result: Pioneers: lichens, then mosses

content.question: After a bush fire clears shrubs near Ogbomosho, which stage will appear first, and what will the climax be if left undisturbed?
hints: Fire resets succession to grasses
Think of stages after grasses
Climax is stable forest or woodland

lessons.title: Soil Types and Components
lessons.objective: Compare sandy, clayey and loamy soils and explain their components and properties important for plant growth.

content.heading: Soil Types and Components
paragraphs: At a farm in Nsukka, Musa finds sand in one pit, sticky clay in another, and loam in the third. He wonders why some hold water better. This lesson compares soil types and explains components.

content.heading: Sandy, Clayey and Loamy Soils
paragraphs: Soils differ because their particles differ in size. Sandy soil has large particles, big air spaces and high porosity, so water drains quickly. Clayey soil has tiny particles, small pores and low porosity, so it holds water for a long time.

Sandy soil warms quickly and is easy to work, but it dries fast and holds few nutrients. Clayey soil is heavy, sticky when wet and hard when dry, and it is poorly aerated. Roots struggle to get air in clayey soil after heavy rain.

Loamy soil has a mixture of sand, silt and clay, so it balances the qualities of both. It has good porosity, holds water well and allows air for roots. For these reasons, loamy soil is the best for most crops in a farm.
bullets: Sandy: large particles, drains fast, poorly holds water
Clayey: tiny particles, holds water, poorly aerated
Loamy: mixed particles, good water and air balance
content.takeaway: Particle size controls porosity, water retention and aeration in sandy, clayey and loamy soils.

check.question: Which soil drains water fastest and is poorest in water retention?
check.why: Sandy soil has large particles and big pores, so water drains away quickly.

content.heading: Soil Structure, Porosity and Capillarity
paragraphs: Soil structure describes how particles are arranged into crumbs or clumps with spaces between them. Good structure creates pores that allow roots, air and water to move freely. Poor structure compacts the soil and reduces pore space in a fertile topsoil.

Porosity is the amount of pore space in the soil, and it affects drainage and aeration. Capillarity is the rise of water through narrow tubes or pores against gravity. In soil, capillarity draws water upward from moist layers to dry roots.

Humus improves structure by binding particles into crumbs and holding water and nutrients. Soils rich in humus are darker, more porous and more fertile. Capillarity and humus together help roots obtain steady water even in dry spells.
bullets: Structure: arrangement of particles into crumbs with pores
Porosity: pore space for air and water movement
Capillarity: water rises in narrow pores to roots
content.takeaway: Good structure, porosity and capillarity give roots steady water, air and nutrients.

check.question: Capillarity in soil means
options: Water flows down by gravity only
Water rises through narrow pores to roots
Air moves out of the soil
check.why: Capillarity is the upward movement of water through narrow tubes or pores, helping roots absorb water.

content.heading: Components of Soil
paragraphs: Soil has inorganic components and organic components. Inorganic components are mineral particles from weathered rock, plus soil water and soil air in the pores. Mineral particles vary from sand to clay and determine soil type.

Organic components include humus, living roots and dead remains of plants and animals. Humus comes from decayed organic matter and darkens the soil. Roots add organic matter as they die and provide channels for air and water.

Soil organisms such as earthworms, bacteria and fungi break down organic matter and release nutrients. Earthworms burrow and aerate the soil, while bacteria and fungi decompose remains. Soil air contains oxygen for roots and organisms, and carbon dioxide from respiration.
bullets: Inorganic: mineral particles, soil water and soil air
Organic: humus, roots and dead organic matter
Organisms: earthworms, bacteria and fungi release nutrients
content.takeaway: Soil combines minerals, water, air, humus and organisms that support plant growth.

check.question: Which group lists only inorganic components of soil?
options: Mineral particles, soil water and air
check.why: Mineral particles, soil water and soil air are inorganic, while the others include organic matter.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For JAMB, link particle size to behaviour: sandy drains fast, clayey holds water, loamy balances both. Recall capillarity draws water upward in narrow pores, and soil air supplies oxygen to roots and soil organisms for respiration.

content.problem: A farmer in Makurdi has sandy soil that dries quickly. He adds compost and clay in small amounts. Explain why the change improves water retention and aeration for his yams.

steps.operation: Identify the problem: sandy soil has large particles and big pores
